Physics is the branch of science that involves the study of the physical world in specific and physical universe in general: energy, matter, and how they are related. In physics modeling of the natural world is made with theory, and is usually expressed quantitatively with mathematical description.
Measurement

Even if we do not study PHYSICS as a subject we depend on it for nearly everything. From walking to driving a car, from cooking to using a gadget, from cutting a tree to building a new house everything involves physics. Even as we read this sentence, physics is at work.
Measurement
Physicists investigate the motions of electrons and rockets, the energy in sound waves and electric circuits, the structure of the proton and that of the universe.
Measurement

Physics is also called ‘the fundamental science’ because the subject of study of all branches of natural science like chemistry, astronomy, geology, and biology are constrained by laws of physics. We can say ‘All other natural sciences stem from physics. Chemistry is essentially applied physics and biology is applied chemistry’.
Measurement

For technologies to develop physics is essential. Physics generates fundamental knowledge needed for the future technological advances that will continue to drive the economic engines of the world. So many pivotal discoveries of the 20th century - including the laser, television, radio, computer technology plus internet, DNA and nuclear weapons are all credited to advancement in physics.
Measurement

Physics contributes to the technological infrastructure and provides trained personnel needed to take advantage of scientific advances and discoveries. It is important for improvement in health, telecommunication, transport and design of our future. Nearly all consumer goods we use at home have been developed from research in physics.
Measurement

The International System of Units (abbreviated SI from système internationale , the French version of the name) is a scientific method of expressing the magnitudes or quantities of important natural phenomena.
Measurement
Science require that quantities must be defined and measured. Things that cannot be measured like beauty, love, hate, are all not science.
Measurement
On the other hand quantities like length, time, density, temperature, electric fluxes can be measured therefore they are called physical quantities.
Measurement
A complete set of units for all physical quantities is called system of units.
Measurement

However to form a system we does not need to define every quantity. We take only a few quantities (called base quantities) and base units to agree on accessible and invariable standards for measurement such that all other quantities and units are expressed in terms of those quantities.

A vector is a mathematical quantity having both magnitude and direction. Some quantities (such as weight, velocity, or friction) require both a magnitude (or size) and a direction for a complete description and are called vectors. Vectors, having both magnitude and direction, obey the rules of vector algebra. Unlike scalars, they cannot be added, subtracted and multiplied by using ordinary algebra.

Graphically a vector is represented by an arrow, the length of the arrow gives the magnitude (under certain scale) and the arrow head points the direction of the vector.

Motion is very important as nearly every physical process involve some kind of motion. Mechanics is the branch of science that deals with the study of motion of bodies, which is further sub-divided into kinematics and dynamics. In this chapter we start our discussion from kinematics, which explains the motion without making any reference to the force (cause of motion).

Later, this discussion is extended to dynamics, which deals with the study of motion under the action of force and its various types.

For example a body in moving train is in motion with respect to an observer on ground. Whereas the same object is at rest with respect to another observer in train. WORK. Work has a different meaning in physics than it does in everyday usage. In physics, work is done only if an object is moved through some displacement while a force is applied to it. For example, if person holding a heavy chair at arm's length, for 3 min. His tired arms may lead him to think that he has done a considerable amount of work on the chair. However, he has done no work on it whatsoever.
Work and Energy

He exerts a force to support the chair, but do not move it. Work is a scalar quantity. Work may be done by constant force as well as by a variable force. Here we start with work done using constant force.
Work and Energy

When we apply some force F on a body and if the body moves through some distance in the direction of force, then the product of force F and displacement d is called work: W = F⃗ · d⃗. In Figure 4.1, a person pulling a crate with a force that is at an angle θ, relative to the direction of the motion. In the diagram beside the sketch, you can see that the x-component (horizontal) of the force has a magnitude F cos θ.
Work and Energy
This component is in the direction of the motion and is the only component that is doing work.
Work and Energy

The y-component (vertical) is perpendicular to the direction of the motion and does no work on the crate. The body is displaced by d⃗. We have resolved F⃗ into its components F⃗ₓ and F⃗ᵧ. The body is displaced by force Fₓ, so work is done by Fₓ: W = Fₓd = (F cos θ)d = Fd cos θ, or W = Fd cos θ. Here W = Fdₓ = F(d cos θ) = Fd cos θ. Thus, W = F⃗ · d⃗.
Work and Energy
FIGURE 4.1. The only component of the force acting on an object that does work is the component that is parallel to the direction of the displacement.
Work and Energy

Figure 4.2: shows four special cases that will clarify the question of whether work is being done by a force. In Figure 4.2 (a) a person is pushing a cart with a force (F) that is in the same direction as the motion of the cart. W = F · Δd = FΔd cos 0° = FΔd. Thus positive work is done on the cart, increasing its kinetic energy.
Work and Energy

In Figure 4.2(b), the direction of the force exerted on the cart is opposite to the direction of motion. W = F · Δd = FΔd cos 180° = −FΔd; θ = 180°, cos θ = −1. Thus negative work is done on the cart, slowing it down and reducing its kinetic energy.
Work and Energy

In part of Figure 4.2 (c) the person is sitting on the cart, exerting a downward force while cart has horizontal motion. W = F · Δd = FΔd cos 90° = 0; θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0. Even though the cart is moving, this force does no work because it is not directly affecting the cart’s horizontal motion.
Work and Energy

Finally, in part (d), the person is pushing on the cart, but the cart is not moving. W = F · Δd = FΔd cos 0°; d = 0, so W = 0. Thus the person is not doing work on the cart, because the displacement is zero.
Work and Energy

4.1.1 WORK DONE BY A CONSTANT FORCE. When a constant force acts through a distance d, the event can be plotted on a simple graph (Figure 4.3). Distance is normally plotted along the x-axis and force along the y-axis. If constant force F and displacement d are in the same direction, work done is Fd, shown by the shaded area in Figure 4.3.

Hence the area under a force-displacement curve can represent the work done by the force. “Work is said to be 1 J if a force of 1 newton displaces a body by 1 metre in the direction of force.” If force is 1 N and d = 1 m, then W = 1 N · 1 m = 1 J.
Work and Energy

4.1.2 WORK DONE BY A VARIABLE FORCE. In many cases the force does not remain constant during the process of doing work. For example: (i) As a rocket moves away from Earth, work is done against gravity, which varies as the inverse square of distance from Earth’s centre; the force decreases and does not remain constant.

(ii) The force exerted by a spring increases with the amount of stretch (pulling), so the force does not remain constant. While considering W = Fₓd cos θ for measurement of work, we suppose that Fₓ is constant throughout displacement d. We shall now consider work done by a force that is not constant. Work done by a varying force can be determined graphically.
Work and Energy

To do so, we plot the force Fₓ as a function of distance Δd, as in Figure 4.4. We divide the distance Δd into small segments. For each segment, we indicate the average of Fₓ by a horizontal dashed line. Then the work done for each segment is ΔW = FₓΔd, the area of a rectangle Δd wide and Fₓ high, as shown in Figure 4.5.
Work and Energy

The total work done to move the object a total distance Δd = dᵦ − dₐ is the sum of the areas of the rectangles (five in the case shown in Figure 4.5). Usually the average value of Fₓ for each segment must be estimated, and a reasonable approximation of the work done can then be made. If we subdivide the distance into many more segments, Δd can be made smaller and our estimate of the work done would be more accurate.
Work and Energy

In Figure 4.5 the path of a body in the xy-plane is shown as it moves from point A to point B. We have divided the whole distance into a number of small displacements Δd₁, Δd₂, Δd₃, …, Δdₙ, respectively, and the corresponding forces are F⃗ₓ₁, F⃗ₓ₂, F⃗ₓ₃, …, F⃗ₓₙ. Total work done in this case is W = ΔW₁ + ΔW₂ + ΔW₃ + … + ΔWₙ = (Fₓ₁ cos θ₁)Δd₁ + (Fₓ₂ cos θ₂)Δd₂ + … + (Fₓₙ cos θₙ)Δdₙ, or W = Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Fₓᵢ cos θᵢ)Δdᵢ.
Work and Energy

In the limit as Δd approaches zero, the total area of the many narrow rectangles approaches the area under the curve in Figure 4.5. That is, the work done by a variable force in moving an object between two points is equal to the area under the Fₓ versus Δd curve between those two points: Wₜ = lim(Δd→0) Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Fₓᵢ cos θᵢ)Δdᵢ.
Work and Energy

4.2 WORK DONE IN GRAVITATIONAL FIELD. We know that a body placed in the space surrounding Earth experiences a force equal to its weight and directed towards the centre of Earth, as shown in Figure 4.6. This space around Earth within which it exerts a force of attraction on other bodies is known as the gravitational field. The gravitational force per unit mass on a body is known as gravitational field strength.
Work and Energy

Its SI unit is N kg⁻¹. If we carry a body in a closed path in such a field, the total work done will be zero. Such a field is known as conservative. In a gravitational field, the work done is independent of the path followed by a body in a closed path.
Work and Energy

Let us consider a closed path ABCA in a gravitational field, as shown in Figure 4.7. A body of mass m and weight w is carried along the closed path from C to B and then from B to A. The angle between w and d₂ is 90°, and the angle between BA and w is 180°. The angle between BA and AC is θ.
Work and Energy

Now we have to calculate the total work done. (i) Work done between C and B: ΔWc→b = w·d₂ = wd₂ cos 90° = 0. (ii) Work done between B and A: ΔWb→a = wd₁ cos 180° = −wd₁. (iii) Work done between A and C: ΔWa→c = wd cos θ = w(d cos θ) (i). From the right-angle triangle, d₁ = d cos θ. Then Eq. (i) becomes ΔWa→c = w(d cos θ) = wd₁, so ΔWa→c = wd₁.
Work and Energy

Total work done in closed path ACBA is Wₜ = ΔWc→b + ΔWb→a + ΔWa→c. Putting the values, Wₜ = 0 + (−wd₁) + wd₁ = 0; thus Wₜ = 0. Since total work done in the closed path ACBA in a gravitational field is zero, the gravitational field is a conservative field.
Work and Energy

FOR YOUR INFORMATION. Conservative forces are: electric force, elastic spring force, and gravitational force. Non-conservative forces are: frictional forces, air resistance, tension in a string, normal force, propulsion force of a motor, and propulsion force of a rocket.
Work and Energy

Now consider Figure 4.8. Let the body be displaced in a gravitational field by two different paths. (i) Work done in path (1) from A to C: Wₜ = wd cos θ; from the figure, d cos θ = d₁. So Wₜ = w(d cos θ) = wd₁.
Work and Energy
(ii) Work done in path (2) from A to B and B to C.
Work and Energy

From A to B, work done is ΔWa→b = wd₁ cos 0° = wd₁. From B to C, ΔWb→c = wd₂ cos 90° = 0. So total work done using the indirect path is Wₜ = ΔWa→b + ΔWb→c = wd₁ + 0 = wd₁. Comparing (i) and (ii), we conclude that work done on a body between any two points in a gravitational field is independent of the path followed by the body. Thus the gravitational field is conservative.
Work and Energy
Electrostatic and magnetic fields are also examples.

4.3 POWER. Machines may be classified by the speed with which they transfer energy or do work. No time factor is involved in the definition of work. The same amount of work may be done by one agency in a small interval of time, say one second, while it may be done by another agency in a much larger time, say one hour. From daily experience, we can say that the former agency has more power than the latter one.
Work and Energy

Power is defined as the rate of transfer of energy. The amount of work done by a body in one second is called power. If W is the work done by a body in time t, then P = W/t. Putting W = F⃗ · d⃗, then P = F⃗ · d⃗/t = F⃗ · v⃗.
Work and Energy

Thus we can say the dot product of force and velocity is called power. (i) “The total work ΔW done by a body in total time Δt is called average power.” Pₐᵥ = (total work done)/(total time) = F⃗ · v⃗ₐᵥ / Δt. (ii) “The rate of doing work in any instant of time is called instantaneous power.” Pᵢₙₛₜ = lim(Δt→0)(ΔW/Δt).
Work and Energy

Anyone may find the power he or she is able to develop when running upstairs by measuring the total vertical height of a stairway and using a stopwatch to find the time taken. The unit of power is called watt. Power is said to be one watt if one joule of work is done by a body in 1 second: 1 watt = J s⁻¹. A watt is a very small unit; usually we use kilowatts: 1 kW = 1000 watts.
Work and Energy

Watt is commonly used for the power of bulbs and electric fans. The power of generating stations and grid stations is expressed in megawatts (1 MW = 10⁶ watts). We usually use the unit kilowatt-hour (1 kWh), the commercial unit of work (electrical energy). Sometimes work is expressed as watt-second. A commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt-hour.
Work and Energy

One kilowatt-hour is the work done in one hour by an agent whose power is one kilowatt: 1 kWh = 1000 watts × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ. The power of a TV set is 120 watts and that of a pocket calculator is 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ watts. FOR YOUR INFORMATION: In the British Engineering system, the unit of power is called horsepower (hp) and numerically, 1 hp = 746 watts.
Work and Energy

Whenever we do work on a body, we store in it an amount of energy equal to the work done. Thus energy is defined as: “The capacity of a body to do work,” or “Energy is the agent which causes some change in the state of a system.” (i) KINETIC ENERGY.
Work and Energy
We observe daily that a moving object has the ability to push away another object at rest. Thus it has the capacity to do work because of its motion. Thus kinetic energy is defined as:

Energy in the body is due to its motion. If m is mass of the body and v⃗ is its velocity, then K.E. = ½mv². (4.4)

(ii) POTENTIAL ENERGY. In daily life we see that if we lift a brick from the ground to the top of a room, work is done against gravity. This appears as potential energy (P.E.) of the brick. Thus P.E. is defined as energy in a body due to its position with respect to the surface of Earth. If m is mass, g is acceleration due to gravity, and h is height of the body from the surface of Earth, then P.E. = mgh. (4.5)

4.5 IMPLICATION OF ENERGY LOSSES IN PRACTICAL DEVICES AND EFFICIENCY. Mechanical efficiency is the ratio of work output to work input. It is often expressed as a percentage. The efficiency of an ideal machine is 100 percent, but an actual machine’s efficiency will always be less than 100%. This means that some of the work put into the system is transformed (lost) into
Work and Energy

Thermal energy (heat). In a mechanical system, friction is the most common cause of energy lost to heat. FIGURE 4.11 · CRANE. The crane is a machine used in daily life to lift heavy loads. It uses three simple machines: a pulley, lever, and wheel and axle. Suppose a weight W is raised using a pulley when an effort/force E is applied.
Work and Energy

OUTPUT. If a machine moves a load W through a distance h, the useful work done by the machine is called output: Output = load × distance h through which the load moves = Fₒᵤₜ × Dₒᵤₜ. INPUT. If an effort Fᵢₙ acts through a distance Dᵢₙ, the work done on the machine is called input: Input = effort force × effort distance = Fᵢₙ × Dᵢₙ.
Work and Energy

EFFICIENCY. The ratio of output to input of a machine is called its efficiency. Efficiency = output work/input work = (load force × load distance)/(effort force × effort distance) = (Fₒᵤₜ × Dₒᵤₜ)/(Fᵢₙ × Dᵢₙ). (4.6) Percentage efficiency = (output work/input work) × 100% = (Wₒᵤₜ/Wᵢₙ) × 100% = (Fₒᵤₜ × Dₒᵤₜ)/(Fᵢₙ × Dᵢₙ) × 100%.
Work and Energy
(4.7) Even a very efficient device will waste some of its input energy as heat due to friction between different parts of the machine.

4.6 ABSOLUTE POTENTIAL ENERGY. Consider a body of mass m at height h in a gravitational field. Its potential energy is P.E. = mgh. When h of a body of mass m is greater than the radius of Earth, the above equation is not applicable. Thus the absolute value of the potential energy of a body in a gravitational field is needed. For this purpose the zero point for potential energy is fixed.
Work and Energy
The zero point is so far away from Earth that the force of gravity is negligibly small and the body is not attracted by Earth. Hence its potential energy is zero.
Work and Energy

To compute the work done in moving a body of mass m from Earth’s surface to a very far-off distance, where gravity is reduced, consider Figure 4.12. A body of mass m is at point 1, at distance r₁ from the centre of Earth. As the body moves from point 1 to a far-off point n, gravitational force does not remain constant.
Work and Energy
Therefore divide the whole distance into small distances, each of magnitude Δr, so the force during each interval remains constant.
Work and Energy

(i) Work done between points 1 and 2: ΔW₁→₂ = Fₐᵥ Δr = Fₐᵥ(r₂ − r₁). (i) But Fₐᵥ = GmMₑ/rₐᵥ², where rₐᵥ = (r₁ + r₂)/2. Then ΔW₁→₂ = (GmMₑ/rₐᵥ²)(r₂ − r₁). (ii) ΔW₁→₂ = (GmMₑ/(r₁r₂))(r₂ − r₁), putting the values. Therefore ΔW₁→₂ = GmMₑ(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Work and Energy

FORMULA DERIVATION. As rₐᵥ = (r₁ + r₂)/2, but Δr = r₂ − r₁ and r₂ = r₁ + Δr, then rₐᵥ = (2r₁ + Δr)/2. Squaring both sides and neglecting Δr², we get rₐᵥ² = r₁r₂. Similarly, ΔW₂→₃ = GmMₑ(1/r₂ − 1/r₃), and ΔW₃→₄ = GmMₑ(1/r₃ − 1/r₄), continuing for successive intervals.
Work and Energy

For successive intervals, ΔWₙ₋₂→ₙ₋₁ = GmMₑ(1/rₙ₋₂ − 1/rₙ₋₁) and ΔWₙ₋₁→ₙ = GmMₑ(1/rₙ₋₁ − 1/rₙ). Adding all these gives ΔW₁→ₙ = ΔW₁→₂ + ΔW₂→₃ + ΔW₃→₄ + … + ΔWₙ₋₂→ₙ₋₁ + ΔWₙ₋₁→ₙ. Putting corresponding values, the terms cancel successively, resulting in ΔW₁→ₙ = GmMₑ(1/r₁ − 1/rₙ). (iii)
Work and Energy

If the nth point N lies at infinity, then rₙ = ∞, and (iii) becomes ΔW₁→∞ = GmMₑ(1/r₁ − 1/∞) = GmMₑ/r₁. (iv) If we displace the body from Earth’s surface, of radius Rₑ, replace r₁ by Rₑ: ΔW = GmMₑ/Rₑ. Thus, from Earth’s surface up to infinity, absolute potential energy = GmMₑ/Rₑ.
Work and Energy

Actually, this is work done against gravity, so its value is always taken as negative. Absolute potential energy = −GmMₑ/Rₑ. (4.8) Gravitational potential at any point is defined as the potential energy per unit mass at that point, which is at distance r from the centre of Earth: V(r) = −GMₑ/r. (4.9)

4.7 ESCAPE VELOCITY. If a body is projected upward, it returns to the ground due to gravity. If its initial velocity is increased, it takes longer to fall back. If initial velocity keeps increasing, a stage is reached when the body will never come back, but will escape the influence of gravity.

The initial velocity a projectile must have at Earth’s surface to go out of Earth’s gravitational field is known as escape velocity. As Earth’s gravitational field extends to infinity, escape velocity is the velocity a projectile must have at Earth’s surface to reach an infinite distance in space.

FIGURE · A Delta II rocket blasting off. A rocket going into space needs a large amount of energy to achieve escape velocity, leave Earth, and get into space.

The work done in lifting a body from Earth’s surface to a very far distance into space, the absolute potential energy at Earth’s surface, is G Mₑm/Rₑ. Where Mₑ is Earth’s mass and Rₑ is Earth’s radius. If a projectile is given initial kinetic energy equal to G Mₑm/Rₑ, it will reach an infinite distance from Earth and have escape velocity. Equating initial K.E. with absolute potential energy:
Work and Energy
½mv²ₑₛ꜀ = GMₑm/Rₑ, so vₑₛ꜀ = √(2GMₑ/Rₑ). (4.10) As GMₑ/Rₑ² = g, GMₑ = gRₑ². Substituting in Eq. 4.10 gives vₑₛ꜀ = √(2gRₑ). (4.11)

4.8 WORK-ENERGY THEOREM IN RESISTIVE MEDIUM. Energy can be stored in one of two basic types: kinetic energy and potential energy. One form can be converted into the other. When a hammer is raised to a certain height h, it acquires gravitational potential energy. Its
Work and Energy

Gravitational potential energy can be used to drive a nail into wood. If a hammer of weight w is released, it falls under gravity and does work on the nail by driving it into the wood block (Figure 4.14). Work done = w × h. Under gravity, a hammer loses potential energy and acquires kinetic energy while falling. Just before hitting the ground, its potential energy is minimum and kinetic energy maximum.
Work and Energy
Assume energy transformation is frictionless: acquiring kinetic energy = loss in potential energy = work done = wh = mgh. (4.12)
Work and Energy

The potential energy lost by the hammer falling from B to A equals the kinetic energy gained when it reaches A. Thus potential energy decreases when an equal increase in kinetic energy occurs. In many situations friction cannot be ignored. Frictional forces reduce mechanical energy (but not total energy), so they are called dissipative forces.
Work and Energy

Work done by friction makes energy transformation imperfect; friction causes energy loss. Part of potential energy is used against friction (fh), and the remaining potential energy becomes kinetic energy: mgh = fh + ½mv². (4.13) Loss in potential energy = gain in kinetic energy + work done against friction. When a body moves up, loss in K.E. at A = gain in P.E. at B + work done against friction.
Work and Energy
This leads to the law of conservation of energy in terms of K.E. and P.E.
Work and Energy

4.9 CONSERVATION OF ENERGY. Kinetic and potential energies are different forms of the same basic quantity, i.e. mechanical energy. Total mechanical energy of a body is the sum of its kinetic energy and potential energy. In our previous

discussion of a falling body, potential energy may change into kinetic energy and vice versa, but the total energy remains constant. Mathematically, Total Energy = P.E. + K.E. = Constant. This is a special case of the law of conservation of energy: “Energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
Work and Energy

It can be transformed from one form into another, but the total amount of energy remains constant.” This is one of the basic laws of physics. We daily observe energy transformations from one form to another.
Work and Energy

Some forms, such as electrical and chemical energy, are more easily transferred than others, such as heat. Ultimately, all energy transfers result in heating of the environment and energy is wasted. For example, the P.E. of a falling object changes to K.E.; on striking the ground, K.E. changes into heat and sound.
Work and Energy
If it seems in an energy transfer that some energy has disappeared, the lost energy is often converted into heat.

5.3 CENTRIPETAL FORCE AND CENTRIPETAL ACCELERATION
Rotational and Circular Motion
If a moving object has no forces acting on it, it will continue to move in a straight line at constant velocity.
Rotational and Circular Motion
The direction of velocity of a body changes. Change in velocity produces acceleration directed toward the centre of the circle. This is called centripetal acceleration.
Rotational and Circular Motion

In Figure 5.7, consider a body of mass m moving in a circle of radius r with uniform speed v. C is the centre of the circle. At point A at time t₁, the velocity of the body is v⃗₁, and at point B at time t₂, its velocity is v⃗₂. Let us draw a triangle PQR such that PQ is equal and parallel to v⃗₁ and PR is equal and parallel to v⃗₂.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Since speed is uniform, |v⃗₁| = |v⃗₂| = v, but they differ in direction. By the vector diagram, Δv⃗ = v⃗₂ − v⃗₁ is the change in velocity of the body in the time interval Δt = t₂ − t₁. When Δt is small, Δv is small and arc AB is approximately equal to chord AB. The triangles ΔACB and ΔPQR are isosceles and similar. Geometrically, arc AB / AC = QR / PQ; or S / r = Δv / v.
Rotational and Circular Motion

When θ is very small, or Δt = t₂ − t₁ is very small, point B is very near point A and S = vt. Then vΔt / r = Δv / v (provided Δt is very very small), or Δv / Δt = v² / r. In the limit Δt → 0, Δv / Δt = ainst; therefore ainst = v² / r.
Rotational and Circular Motion
This acceleration is also called centripetal acceleration. Thus ac = v² / r. Vectorially, a⃗c = (v² / r) r̂ (5.7).
Rotational and Circular Motion

Here r⃗ is the radius vector directing outward from the centre of the circle. From Figure 5.8, ac and r⃗ are oppositely directed. Hence a⃗c = −(v² / r²) r⃗ (5.8). The direction of a⃗ at each instant is perpendicular to velocity and toward the centre of the circle.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Using the previous relation v = rω, where ω is angular velocity, the angular form of centripetal acceleration is a⃗c = −ω² r⃗ (5.9). Using Newton’s 2nd law, Fc = mac, where Fc is centripetal force. Putting ac = v² / r, the force relation continues on the next page.
Rotational and Circular Motion
We get centripetal force Fc = mv² / r (5.10). Similarly, in vector form F⃗c = −(mv² / r²) r⃗, and in angular form F⃗c = −(mω²) r⃗.

Rotational and Circular Motion

It is easier to throw a small stone than a heavier one. The heavier one has more mass and therefore resists more. Inertia in a body is due to its mass. Thus inertia is the property of an object to resist change in its state of rest or motion.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Similarly in rotational motion, moment of inertia is the property by which a body resists change in its state of rotatory motion. Moment of inertia plays the same role in rotational motion as mass does in translational motion. When force is applied to a bicycle wheel, angular acceleration is produced.

The greater the force, the greater the angular acceleration produced. The more massive the wheel, the smaller the angular acceleration. Pushing on a spoke closer to the axle gives smaller angular acceleration. If force F acts on a point mass m at distance r from the axle, then a = rα, where α is angular acceleration. Substituting in F = ma gives F = mrα.

Since torque is the turning effect of force, and F acts perpendicular to r, torque is τ = Fr or τ = mr²α (5.12).

The above equation is the rotational analogue of Newton’s second law (F = ma). The quantity I = mr² is called rotational inertia or moment of inertia of a point mass m at distance r from the centre of rotation. Putting I = mr² in Eq. (5.12), thus τ = Iα (5.13).
Rotational and Circular Motion
The product of moment of inertia I and angular acceleration α of a body gives the magnitude of the torque acting on it.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Consider a rigid body as shown in Figure 5.14. Divide the whole body into small pieces with masses m₁, m₂, …, mₙ and radii r₁, r₂, …, rₙ from its centre of gravity. In this case, I = m₁r₁² + m₂r₂² + … + mₙrₙ², or I = Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ mᵢrᵢ² (5.14). This is the moment of inertia of the given rigid body.
Rotational and Circular Motion
EXAMPLE 5.4. A 2 kg mass swings in a circle of radius 50 cm at the end of a light rod. What resultant torque is required to give an angular acceleration of 2.5 rad/s²?
Rotational and Circular Motion
GIVEN. Radius r = 50 cm = 0.5 m; mass m = 2 kg; angular acceleration α = 2.5 rad/s².
Rotational and Circular Motion
SOLUTION. I = mR² = (2 kg)(0.5 m)² = 0.5 kg m². τ = Iα = (0.5 kg m²)(2.5 rad/s²) = 1.25 N m. Answer: 1.25 N m.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Rotational and Circular Motion

Rotational and Circular Motion
5.5 ANGULAR MOMENTUM AND TORQUE
Rotational and Circular Motion
Torque exerted by a force produces rotation or changes the rotation of a particle or an extended body about an axis of rotation. In other words, torque produces angular acceleration α in a body.
Rotational and Circular Motion
The torque τ⃗ exerted by a force F⃗ acting on a particle at position vector r⃗ from the axis of rotation is defined as τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗ (i).
Rotational and Circular Motion

Figure 5.16 shows a particle at position vector r⃗ with linear momentum p⃗ = mv⃗. Angular momentum L⃗ is the cross-product of r⃗ and p⃗ and is perpendicular to the plane containing them: L⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗ = r⃗ × mv⃗ (5.15).
Rotational and Circular Motion

The magnitude of angular momentum follows from the cross-product definition: L = rp sin θ, where θ is the angle between r⃗ and p⃗. Its direction is perpendicular to the plane formed by r⃗ and p⃗. Its units are kg m² s⁻¹ or, more commonly, joule-seconds.
Rotational and Circular Motion

For motion in a circle, r⃗ is always perpendicular to p⃗. Momentum p⃗ is tangential to the circle all along its circumference. Then L = rp sin 90° = rp. Since r is constant, any change in L is brought about only by a change in p = mv.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Consider a rigid object rotating about a fixed axis that coincides with the z-axis of a coordinate system, as shown in Figure 5.17. Let us determine the angular momentum of this object, made up of small mass segments. All mass segments undergo circular motion about the z-axis with the same angular velocity ω⃗.
Rotational and Circular Motion

The rigid body is made of many particles, and the sum of the angular momenta of all the particles gives its total angular momentum. In terms of the masses and velocities of individual particles, L = Σi mi Ri vi = Σi mi Ri²ω, since v = Rω. The summation Σi mi Ri² is the moment of inertia I of the rigid body about the axis of rotation.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Thus, L = Σi (mi Ri²)ω = Iω. The magnitude of the angular momentum along the axis of rotation of a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω about the axis is L = Iω.
Rotational and Circular Motion
EXAMPLE 5.5. Find Earth’s angular momentum using the Earth–Sun distance and mass of Earth. Earth–Sun distance = 149.6 × 10⁹ m. Mass of Earth = 5.9742 × 10²⁴ kg.
Rotational and Circular Motion
GIVEN. Mean distance from Earth to Sun = 149.6 × 10⁹ km; mass of Earth Me = 5.9742 × 10²⁴ kg.
Rotational and Circular Motion
REQUIRED. Angular momentum L = ?
Rotational and Circular Motion

SOLUTION. For a circular orbit, angular momentum is L⃗ = r⃗ × Me v⃗. The average angular momentum is Me v r, treating Earth as a point mass. Earth takes 365 days to complete one circle around the Sun.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Rotational and Circular Motion
Average angular momentum L = Me v r = (5.9742 × 10²⁴ kg)(2.98 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹)(149.6 × 10⁹ m) = 2.663 × 10⁴⁰ kg m² s⁻¹. Answer: Earth’s angular momentum is 2.663 × 10⁴⁰ kg m² s⁻¹.
Rotational and Circular Motion

FOR YOUR INFORMATION. Our solar system was born from a huge cloud of gas and dust that initially had rotational energy. Gravitational forces caused the cloud to contract, and the rotation rate increased as a result of conservation of angular momentum.
Rotational and Circular Motion

The solar system coalesced from a cloud of gas and dust that was originally rotating. The orbital motions and spins of the planets are in the same direction as the original spin and conserve the angular momentum of the parent cloud.
Rotational and Circular Motion

5.6 CONSERVATION OF ANGULAR MOMENTUM
Rotational and Circular Motion
In Chapter 3 we found that the total linear momentum of a system of particles remains constant if the system is isolated. We have an analogous conservation law in rotational motion:
Rotational and Circular Motion
The total angular momentum of a system is constant in both magnitude and direction if the resultant external torque acting on the system is zero, that is, if the system is isolated.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Consider again Eq. (ii): the change in angular momentum is ΔL⃗ = r⃗ × Δp⃗. Dividing both sides by the change in time Δt gives ΔL⃗ / Δt = r⃗ × (Δp⃗ / Δt) = r⃗ × F⃗ = τ⃗. Thus the rate of change of angular momentum is equal to torque. Although derived for circular motion, this equation is true in general: ΔL⃗ / Δt = τ⃗ (5.16).
Rotational and Circular Motion

For an isolated system, τ⃗ = 0. Therefore, from Eq. (5.16), ΔL⃗ / Δt = 0 ⇒ L⃗ = constant (in time). The law of conservation of angular momentum states: In the absence of any external torque, the angular momentum of a system remains constant.
Rotational and Circular Motion
This law is often used by circus acrobats, divers, ballet dancers, ice skaters and others to perform breath-taking feats.
Rotational and Circular Motion

In Figure 5.18, a diver leaves the springboard with arms and legs extended at a small angular speed about a horizontal axis through his centre of gravity. When he pulls his arms and legs in, his moment of inertia becomes smaller. To keep angular momentum constant, his angular velocity increases. He can thus make one or two extra somersaults.
Rotational and Circular Motion

A gymnast starts the dismount at full extension. By tucking in his knees, he brings his mass closer to the centre of the axis of rotation, thereby decreasing the moment of inertia. When the gymnast decreases his moment of inertia, his angular velocity increases in order to keep his angular momentum al… constant. His increased angular velocity allows the gymnast to complete the rotation.
Rotational and Circular Motion
The given Figure (5.20) shows a man standing on a turn table and holding heavy weights in his hands. With arms fully stretched horizontally, he is first set rotating slowly.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Upon drawing the hands and weights in toward the chest, the angular velocity is considerable increased. He can slow down his spinning speed by stretching his hands again. This fact is due to the conservation of angular momentum.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.20. Illustrations of Angular Momentum.
Rotational and Circular Motion
EXAMPLE 5.6. A body of moment of inertia 0.80 kg m² about a fixed axis rotates with constant angular velocity of 100 rad s⁻¹. Calculate: its angular momentum; torque to sustain this position.
Rotational and Circular Motion
GIVEN. Moment of inertia I = 0.80 kg m². Angular velocity ω = 100 rad s⁻¹. REQUIRED. Angular momentum L = ? Torque τ = ?
Rotational and Circular Motion
SOLUTION. For L, use L = Iω. L = 0.80 × 100 = 80 kg m² s⁻¹. As angular velocity is uniform, there is no change in angular velocity and angular acceleration is zero. So τ = Iα = 0.80 × 0 = 0.
Rotational and Circular Motion

5.7 KINETIC ENERGY OF ROTATION. In linear motion, the energy in a body due to its linear motion is called K.E. K.E. = ½mv² (5.17), where m is mass of body and v is linear velocity of body. Similarly, the energy in a body due to its angular motion is called rotational kinetic energy and is given by equation K.E.rot = ½Iω².
Rotational and Circular Motion

Let I be the moment of inertia of a body and ω its angular velocity. Divide the rigid body into small masses m₁, m₂, …, mₙ at distances r₁, r₂, …, rₙ from its C.G. The total K.E. is K.E.₁ + K.E.₂ + … + K.E.ₙ = ½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂² + … + ½mₙvₙ². Using v = rω, K.E.rot = ½m₁r₁²ω² + ½m₂r₂²ω² + … + ½mₙrₙ²ω². Each piece is assumed to move with the same angular velocity. Thus K.E.rot = ½ω²(Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ mᵢrᵢ²).
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.21. Each particle in the object has kinetic energy as the object moves.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Since Σᵢ₌₁ⁿmᵢrᵢ² = I, K.E.rot = ½Iω² (5.18).
Rotational and Circular Motion

Comparing angular and linear motions. The corresponding equations are shown in Figure/table: S = vt ↔ θ = ωt; vᶠ = vᵢ + at ↔ ωᶠ = ωᵢ + αt; vᶠ² − vᵢ² = 2aS ↔ ωᶠ² − ωᵢ² = 2αθ; S = vᵢt + ½at² ↔ θ = ωᵢt + ½αt²; inertia m ↔ moment of inertia mr² = I; force ma ↔ torque τ = Iα; momentum p⃗ = mv⃗ ↔ L⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗ or Iω⃗; K.E.lin = ½mv² ↔ K.E.rot = ½Iω².
Rotational and Circular Motion

EXAMPLE 5.7. Calculating the Angular Momentum of a platform. A child of mass 25 kg stands at the edge of a rotating platform of mass 150 kg and radius 4.0 m. The platform with the child on it rotates with angular speed of 6.2 rad/s. The child jumps off in a radial direction. What happens to the angular speed of the platform? Treat the platform as a uniform disk.
Rotational and Circular Motion
GIVEN. Mass of child m₁ = 25 kg; mass of platform m₂ = 150 kg; radius r = 4.0 m; initial angular speed ωᵢ = 6.2 rad s⁻¹. REQUIRED. Final angular speed ωf = ?
Rotational and Circular Motion

SOLUTION. Conservation of angular momentum: The angular momentum of two interacting objects is constant. (Iplatform + Ichild)ωᵢ = Iplatformωf. Iplatform = ½m₂r² = ½(150 kg)(4 m)² = 1200 kg m²; Ichild = m₁r² = 25 kg(4 m)² = 400 kg m².
Rotational and Circular Motion
ωf = [(Iplatform + Ichild)ωᵢ]/Iplatform = [(1200 kg m² + 400 kg m²)(6.2 rad/s)]/(1200 kg m²) = 8.27 rad/s. Answer: 8.27 rad/s.
Rotational and Circular Motion

5.8 ROLLING OF DISC AND HOOP DOWN THE INCLINED PLANE. A piece of thin-walled cylinder or hollow sphere is called a hoop or thin ring. A piece of solid cylinder is called disc, as a carom disc, etc. In Figure 5.22, a disc of mass m and a hoop of mass m are allowed to move along an inclined plane of slope/inclination θ. When they roll down, they have two types of K.E.: linear K.E. (translational) and rotational K.E.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.22. Rolling down of cylinder and hoop on an inclined plane.
Rotational and Circular Motion

For disc or cylinder: when it rolls down, loss in P.E. = gain in K.E.trans + gain in K.E.rot. mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω². From the table, I = ½mR². Then mgh = ½mv² + ¼mR²ω². As v = Rω, mgh = ½mv² + ¼mv² = mv²(½ + ¼).
Rotational and Circular Motion
For the solid disc or cylinder, v = √(4gh/3) (5.19). This is the velocity of the cylinder at the bottom and is independent of its mass. It depends on h, the height of the inclined plane, only.
Rotational and Circular Motion
For hoop: when it rolls down the inclined plane, loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E.lin + Gain in K.E.rot. mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω². mgh = ½mv² + ½mv². From table: I = MR² (for disc). Then gh = v².
Rotational and Circular Motion

For hoop, v = √gh (5.20). This is the velocity of the hoop and is also independent of its mass. Comparing the two velocities, the solid disc will move faster than the hoop and will reach the bottom first.
Rotational and Circular Motion

5.9 THE REAL AND APPARENT WEIGHT. A woman weighs a fish with a spring scale attached to the ceiling of a lift, as shown in the figures. Case 1: lift with zero acceleration. While the lift is at rest, she measures a weight of fish 41.0 N. T = mg = W = 41.0 N, where T is the tension in the string.
Rotational and Circular Motion

The force exerted by the fish on the spring balance equals the pull due to gravity on the object, that is, its weight. The spring-balance reading reflects the true weight W since the lift has no acceleration. Therefore, we call the scale reading the real weight. FIGURE 5.23(a). When the lift is at rest, the spring scale reads the true weight of the fish.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.23(a). When the lift is at rest, the spring scale reads the true weight of the fish.
Rotational and Circular Motion

By Newton’s second law, when acceleration is zero, the resultant force on the object is also zero. If W⃗ is the gravitational force acting on the fish and T⃗ is the tension in the string, then T⃗ = W⃗, or T⃗ − W⃗ = 0 (5.21), as a⃗ = 0.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Case 2. Lift with upward acceleration.
Rotational and Circular Motion

When the lift accelerates upward with acceleration 2.10 m s⁻², tension T⃗ in the string does not equal the downward pull of gravity W⃗. The spring balance reads greater than the actual weight: 49.778 N, as in Figure 5.23(b). This reading is called the apparent weight of the fish. Thus T⃗ > W⃗, and T⃗ = W⃗ + m a⃗ (5.22), where a⃗ is upward acceleration of the elevator.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.23(b). When the lift accelerates upward, the spring scale reads a value greater than the weight of the fish.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Case 3. Lift with downward acceleration.
Rotational and Circular Motion

When the lift accelerates downward with acceleration 2.10 m s⁻², the spring balance reads less than the actual weight W. The lift and fish move downward with acceleration a; the scale reads 32.22 N less than the actual weight, as shown in Figure 5.23(c). Thus W⃗ > T⃗ and T⃗ = W⃗ − m a⃗ (5.23).
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.23(c). When the lift accelerates downward, the spring scale reads a value less than the weight of the fish.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Case 4. Lift falling freely. If the lift falls freely under gravity, then a⃗ = g⃗ and T⃗ = m g⃗ − m g⃗ = 0 (5.24). When the lift falls freely, the spring balance measures zero.
Rotational and Circular Motion

5.10 CONCEPT OF WEIGHTLESSNESS. When the elevator falls with acceleration g, the scale reads the fish’s weight as zero newtons. The fish, scale, and elevator all fall with the same acceleration, so everything in it experiences apparent weightlessness. Weightlessness is a sensation experienced when no external objects touch one’s body and exert a push or pull upon it.
Rotational and Circular Motion
These sensations occur when all contact forces are removed, such as when momentarily in free fall. Gravity is a non-contact force; without opposing forces, one would have no sensation of it.
Rotational and Circular Motion

You would feel weightless when in a state of free fall. Feelings of weightlessness are common at amusement parks for riders of roller coasters and other rides in which riders are momentarily airborne and lifted out of their seats.
Rotational and Circular Motion

5.10.1 FREE FALL IN SPACESHIP. Soon after Newton formulated his law of universal gravitation, he began thinking about experiments about artificial satellites. He reasoned that you could put a cannon at the top of an extremely high mountain and shoot a cannon ball horizontally, as shown in Figure 5.24.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Consider a cannon ball shot parallel to Earth’s horizontal surface from the top of a mountain, ignoring air friction. Gravity pulls the cannon ball downward and it follows path A. Since its speed is too small, it eventually falls to Earth. If it is fired faster, it follows path B and comes down farther away, as illustrated in Figure 5.25.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.24. Cannon ball shot parallel to the horizontal surface of the earth.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.25. Cannon ball fired with a speed of about 8 km s⁻¹.
Rotational and Circular Motion

The curvature of Earth means its surface drops a vertical height of 5 m for every 8000 m tangent to the surface. For a cannon ball to orbit Earth, it should drop vertically 5 m for every 8000 m distance along the horizon. Thus a cannon ball fired with a speed of about 8000 m s⁻¹ will be capable of orbiting.
Rotational and Circular Motion

The cannon ball may travel around the Earth in a circular path and follow path C. When its speed exceeds 8000 m s⁻¹, it overshoots a circular path and travels in an elliptical orbit. A spaceship accelerates toward the centre of Earth at all times, just as the cannon ball orbits Earth; its radial acceleration is g, the free-fall acceleration.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Gravity attracts all objects toward each other and keeps Earth’s natural satellite, the Moon, and its largest artificial satellite, the International Space Station (ISS), in orbit around Earth. A satellite moving in a circle of radius R from the centre of Earth of mass Me has centripetal acceleration aᶜ = g = v²/R. Thus gravity supplies the centripetal acceleration. For a closed orbit, v = √gR (5.25).
Rotational and Circular Motion
With g = 9.8 m s⁻² and Earth’s radius R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, v = 7.9 km s⁻¹ ≈ 8 km s⁻¹ = 8000 m s⁻¹. This is the minimum required velocity to put a satellite into orbit, called critical velocity.
Rotational and Circular Motion

8.11 ARTIFICIAL GRAVITY IN A SPACE STATION. You have probably seen pictures of astronauts in a space capsule, space shuttle, or space station similar to Figure 5.26. The International Space Station, space shuttle, and satellites are designed to stay in orbit, neither falling to the ground nor shooting off into space.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Since the astronaut and station are both falling and nothing holds them up against gravity, they are in free fall and feel weightless.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Weightlessness in a space station is highly inconvenient. The station continuously falls around our planet; astronauts and objects aboard are also in free fall and feel nearly weightless. FIGURE 5.26. Astronauts not in contact with the floor or walls float within the space station.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.26. Astronauts who are not in contact with the floor or walls would be floating within the space station.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Rotational and Circular Motion

POINT TO PONDER. Astronauts in places with microgravity, like on the ISS, are weightless; they can sleep or rest in any orientation. At sleep time, however, they attach themselves so they do not float around and bump into something. ISS astronauts usually sleep in sleeping bags in small crew cabins. Each cabin is just big enough for one person. Astronauts also attach themselves to walls or the ceiling to sleep.
Rotational and Circular Motion

To overcome these problems, space stations might be built as large wheels with hollow rims, as in Figure 5.27. They would rotate so that the outer rim, which acts as the floor, applies a radial centripetal force to occupants and objects inside, keeping them moving in a circle.
Rotational and Circular Motion
FIGURE 5.27. A rotating space station with a hollow rim.
Rotational and Circular Motion

In a rotating space station, people will be “stuck” to the outside too, but with a force equal to gravity, so they can walk around on the edges. The force is the same all around the outside of the rotating cylinder, so depending on the design it could look like people are living on the ceiling. To have a spaceship in space, gravity must be provided to its occupants.
Rotational and Circular Motion
Such provided gravity is called artificial gravity because it does not exist naturally. To produce artificial gravity, the spaceship must rotate with a certain frequency.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Centripetal acceleration is aᶜ = v²/r, where r is the distance from the centre to the rim of the spaceship. For artificial gravity aᶜ = g, so g = rω². In one complete rotation, distance covered = 2πr. The time period is T = 2πr/v = 2πr/(rω) = 2π/ω. Hence ω = 2π/T = 2πf. Then g = r × 4π²f², and f = (1/2π)√(g/r) (5.26).
Rotational and Circular Motion

When the spaceship rotates at this particular frequency, artificial gravity like Earth’s is provided to its inhabitants. Technically, rotation produces the same effect as gravity because it produces a force called centrifugal force. By adjusting parameters such as the radius and rotation rate, a force can be created on the outside walls that equals the force of gravity.
Rotational and Circular Motion

Weather satellites image clouds and measure temperature and rainfall. Both geostationary and low-Earth orbits are used, depending on the type of weather satellite. Weather satellites help with more accurate weather forecasting.

An orbit is a regular, repeating path that one object in space takes around another. An object in an orbit is called a satellite. A satellite may be natural, like Earth’s Moon, or man-made, like the International Space Station.

Consider a satellite of mass ms in a circular orbit about Earth at distance r from its centre. It has centripetal acceleration directed toward Earth’s centre. Earth’s gravity is the only force acting, so Newton’s second law gives the relation shown in Figure 5.30.

For a satellite of mass ms at orbital radius r, ms v²/r = GMe ms/r², where Me is the mass of Earth, ms is the mass of the satellite, and G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Solving for orbital speed gives v = √(GMe/r) (5.27). Since √(GMe) is constant, v ∝ 1/√r (5.28).

5.13 THE GEO-STATIONARY ORBITS. Satellites are launched into different orbits depending on their mission. A common orbit is geostationary: a satellite takes 24 hours to orbit Earth, the same time Earth takes to rotate once on its axis. It stays in the same spot over Earth for communications and television broadcasts. This orbit is ideal for many communications and weather satellites.

A geostationary orbit has an altitude of 22,240 miles (35,790 km), with orbital speed 6,880 mph (11,070 km h⁻¹).

Using Eq. (5.27), orbital speed vo = √(GMe/r₀). This speed equals the satellite’s average speed in one day: vo = s/T = 2πr₀/T, where T is the revolution period, equal to one day. Earth’s gravitational force Fg supplies the centripetal acceleration. In circular orbit acceleration a⃗ is always perpendicular to velocity v⃗, so speed v is constant. Equating the equations gives 2πr₀/T = √(GMe/r₀) (5.29).

Solving gives r₀ = [GMeT²/(4π²)]^(1/3). Putting G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², Me = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, T = 365 × 24 × 3600 s, and π = 3.14, then r₀ = 4.23 × 10⁴ km.

FIGURE 5.31. The satellite is in a circular orbit: its acceleration is always perpendicular to its velocity, so its speed is constant.

This is the orbital radius measured from Earth’s centre for a geostationary satellite. At this height a satellite stays over a particular point on Earth’s surface. Fluid Dynamics

A fluid is a collection of molecules randomly arranged and held together by weak cohesive forces and by forces exerted by the walls of a container. Liquids and gases are fluids because they flow and exert pressure on the walls of a container. Fluids are a subset of the phases of matter and include liquids, gases, plasmas, and to some extent plastic solids.
Fluid Dynamics

6.1 VISCOUS FLUIDS. Viscosity is the resistance to flow of a fluid. Honey has a high viscosity at room temperature, while freely flowing gasoline has a low viscosity. For a fluid to flow, its molecules must slide past one another. In general, the stronger the intermolecular forces of attraction, the more viscous the liquid.
Fluid Dynamics

This internal friction, or viscous force, is associated with the resistance that two adjacent layers of fluid have to move relative to each other. Viscosity causes part of a fluid’s kinetic energy to be converted to internal energy. This mechanism is similar to an object sliding on a rough horizontal surface and losing kinetic energy.
Fluid Dynamics

The numerical value of resistance to fluid flow is called coefficient of viscosity η. The SI unit is the pascal second (Pa s). A common unit is the dyne second per square centimetre (dyne second/cm²), called the poise (P), after French physiologist Jean Louis Poiseuille (1799–1869). 1 pascal second = 10 poise. 1 centipoise = 1 millipascal second. TABLE 6.1. COEFFICIENT OF VISCOSITY OF VARIOUS SUBSTANCES.
Fluid Dynamics

As the temperature of a liquid rises, its atoms become freer to move and the coefficient of viscosity η decreases. In a gas, however, a temperature rise increases the random motion of atoms and the coefficient of viscosity η increases.
Fluid Dynamics

6.2 FLUID FRICTION AND STOKES’ LAW. Fluid friction occurs when adjacent layers in a fluid (liquid or gas) move at different velocities. It depends on the fluid’s viscosity and the relative speeds between fluid layers.
Fluid Dynamics

When an object moves through a fluid, the fluid exerts a retarding force that tends to reduce its speed. This force is called drag. The moving body pushes fluid out of the way; by Newton’s third law, the fluid pushes back on the body with an equal and opposite force. Putting a hand out of a fast-moving car shows fluid friction and drag.
Fluid Dynamics

The drag force depends on: (1) size, shape, and orientation of the object; (2) properties of the fluid (viscosity and density); (3) speed of the object relative to the fluid. POINT TO PONDER. Skydivers and swimmers change their effective size and orientation by bending, twisting, and stretching their body parts. This lets them manipulate drag and control speed and direction of motion.
Fluid Dynamics

The viscous drag force on a spherical object is expressed by Stokes’ law. The drag force Fd depends on radius r, velocity v, and the coefficient of viscosity η of the medium through which the sphere falls. Fd ∝ ηrv, or Fd = Aηrv, where A is a proportionality constant experimentally determined as 6π. Therefore Fd = 6πηrv (6.1).
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.1. Spherical object falling through a medium: radius r, speed v, and coefficient of viscosity η.
Fluid Dynamics

This equation, first set forth by British scientist Sir George G. Stokes in 1851, is termed Stokes’ law. Stokes’ law finds applications in several areas, particularly with regard to settling sediment in fresh water and measurements of the viscosity of fluids.
Fluid Dynamics

6.3 TERMINAL VELOCITY. The constant maximum velocity attained and maintained by an object while falling through a resistive medium is called terminal velocity vT. When net force on an object is zero, acceleration terminates. When acceleration ends, the object has reached terminal speed; for a falling object, its downward terminal velocity vT.
Fluid Dynamics

We consider terminal velocity for the simplest case: a spherical object of uniform density falling through a consistent medium, as in Figure 6.2. Newton’s laws apply whether objects fall freely or in the presence of resistive forces; acceleration differs because the net force differs. In a vacuum, net force is weight alone. With air resistance, net force is weight minus drag.
Fluid Dynamics
Fnet = FG − FD. Here Fnet = ma, FD = 6πηrv, and FG = W = mg. Therefore ma = mg − 6πηrv.
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.2. As a sphere falls, its speed increases and acceleration decreases until terminal velocity vT is reached and acceleration is zero.
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.3. Motion of spherical objects falling through a fluid: drag FD acts upward, weight FG = W = mg acts downward; at terminal velocity the opposing forces balance.
Fluid Dynamics
When FG and FD are equal, net force is zero, acceleration a = 0, and v = vT. The equation becomes m(0) = mg − 6πηr vT, or 0 = mg − 6πηr vT. Therefore 6πηr vT = mg, and vT = mg/(6πηr) (6.2).
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.4. Graphical representation of terminal velocity.
Fluid Dynamics

Equation 6.2 represents the terminal velocity of a spherical object of mass m and radius r falling with acceleration due to gravity g in a medium with coefficient of viscosity η. For a sphere of uniform density, m = ρV (1). The volume of a sphere is V = 4/3 πr³ (2). Substituting V from equation 2 into equation 1 gives m = 4/3 πr³ρ (3).
Fluid Dynamics

Putting m = 4/3 πr³ρ from equation (3) into equation 6.2 and rearranging gives vT = 2ρgr²/(9η) (6.3). Equation 6.3 gives terminal velocity for a spherical object of density ρ and radius r falling under gravity g in a medium with viscosity η.
Fluid Dynamics

Terminal velocity depends on the size, shape, and orientation of an object, and also on the medium’s coefficient of viscosity and speed; therefore there is no single terminal speed. In general, a person falling through Earth’s air reaches terminal velocity after about 12 s, covering about 450 m. TABLE 6.2. Terminal speeds for various objects falling through air.
Fluid Dynamics

Fluid Dynamics

DO YOU KNOW? In free fall, a paratrooper attains terminal velocity twice: once before opening the chute and again after opening it. Without opening the chute the paratrooper has less area facing the air and therefore a high terminal speed. After opening, the chute presents a large area, giving a sufficiently low terminal speed for safe landing. Figure 6.4 explains the motion.
Fluid Dynamics
Stage 1 at t = 0 s: just after jumping from the plane, the skydiver is not moving very fast. Weight is greater than air resistance, so he accelerates downward.
Fluid Dynamics
Stage 2 at t = 19 s: air resistance has increased until it equals the skydiver’s weight. Forces balance and speed remains constant at terminal velocity 1.
Fluid Dynamics
Stage 3 at t = 54 s: when the chute opens, air resistance increases dramatically and becomes much greater than weight, so the skydiver slows down.
Fluid Dynamics
Stage 4 at t = 58 s: as the skydiver slows, drag from the chute decreases until it equals weight. Forces balance and speed remains constant at terminal velocity 2.
Fluid Dynamics

Fluid Dynamics

GIVEN. r = 5.1 × 10⁻⁴ m; η = 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹; density ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³; g = 9.8 m s⁻². REQUIRED. Terminal velocity vT = ? SOLUTION. vT = (2/9)(ρr²g/η) = (2/9)[(1000)(5.1 × 10⁻⁴)²(9.8)/(1.9 × 10⁻⁵)] = 2.98 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹. The fog droplet settles at 0.00298 m/s in air.
Fluid Dynamics

Fluid Dynamics

6.3 FLUID FLOW. When a fluid is in motion, its flow can be characterized as streamline or turbulent. Flow is streamline, steady, or laminar if every fluid particle passing a particular point follows exactly the same path as particles that passed that point earlier.
Fluid Dynamics

In streamline flow every fluid particle follows a smooth path; paths of different particles never cross, as shown in Figure 6.5. A streamline is everywhere tangent to the velocity vector. A stream-tube consists of a bundle of streamlines.
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.5. A streamline is tangent to the velocity vector; a stream-tube consists of a bundle of streamlines.
Fluid Dynamics

Above a certain critical speed, fluid flow becomes turbulent: irregular flow characterized by small whirlpool-like regions. Near incense, smoke flow is smooth or laminar. As smoke rises, it speeds up due to the lower density of warm air than surrounding air (natural convection). As it speeds up, it eventually reaches a speed at which the flow becomes chaotic or turbulent.
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.6. Smoke rising from incense shows laminar flow near the bottom and turbulent flow farther up.
Fluid Dynamics

POINT TO PONDER. Extreme turbulent flow can be seen in a tornado. Tornadoes are violently rotating columns of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground. They can destroy buildings, flip cars, and create deadly flying debris.
Fluid Dynamics

In turbulent flow the speed of the fluid at a point is continuously undergoing changes in both magnitude and direction. Turbulent flow tends to occur at higher velocities and low viscosity, therefore most kinds of fluid flow are turbulent.
Fluid Dynamics

The examples of turbulent flow include blood flow in arteries, oil transport in pipelines, lava flow, atmosphere and ocean currents, the flow through pumps and turbines, and the flow in boat wakes and around aircraft-wing tips.
Fluid Dynamics

POINT TO PONDER. Animals living under water, like fishes, dolphins, and even massive whales are streamlined in shape to reduce drag forces. Birds are streamlined to reduce air drag and migratory species that fly large distances often have particular features such as long necks.
Fluid Dynamics
The discussion of fluid flow can be simplified by considering the fluid flow as ideal flow. In our model of an ideal flow, we make the following assumptions:
Fluid Dynamics

1. THE FLUID IS NON-VISCOUS. In a non-viscous fluid, internal friction is neglected. An object moving through the fluid experiences no viscous force. 2. THE FLOW IS STEADY. In steady (laminar) flow, the velocity of the fluid at each point remains constant. 3. THE FLUID IS INCOMPRESSIBLE. The density of an incompressible fluid is constant. 4. THE FLOW IS IRROTATIONAL.
Fluid Dynamics

In irrotational flow, the fluid has no angular momentum about any point. If a small paddle wheel placed anywhere in the fluid does not rotate about the wheel’s center of mass, then the flow is irrotational. 5. THE TEMPERATURE DOES NOT VARY. Phenomena such as the convection of fluids in which a liquid in the bottom of a vessel is heated, rises, cools, and falls in a circulating pattern will not be considered.
Fluid Dynamics

6.4 EQUATION OF CONTINUITY. The mass of ideal fluid does not change as it flows. This leads to an important quantitative relationship called the continuity equation. The product of cross-sectional area and the speed of the fluid at any point along the pipe is constant. A₁v₁ = A₂v₂; Av = constant (here v is the velocity and A is the area of cross-section).
Fluid Dynamics

FIGURE 6.7. A fluid moving with steady flow through a pipe of varying cross-sectional area. The volume of fluid flowing through area A₁ in a time interval Δt must equal the volume flowing through area A₂ in the same time interval.
Fluid Dynamics

Consider an ideal fluid flowing through a pipe of nonuniform size, as illustrated in Figure 6.7. The particles in the fluid move along streamlines in steady flow. As there is no source or sink in the pipe so equal mass will flow through each end of the pipe. Δm₁ = Δm₂ = Δm (1). By definition of density, ρ = Δm/ΔV or Δm = ρΔV (2). By definition of volume, ΔV = AΔx (3). By definition of average velocity, Δx = vΔt (4).
Fluid Dynamics
Putting value of Δx from equation 4 in equation 3, we get ΔV = AvΔt (5). The fluid that moves through the lower end of the pipe in the time Δt has a mass given by equation 5 as Δm₁ = ρA₁v₁Δt (6).
Fluid Dynamics

The fluid that moves through the upper end of the pipe in the time Δt has a mass given by equation 5 as Δm₂ = ρA₂v₂Δt (7). Putting values from equation 6 and equation 7 in equation 1, we get ρA₁v₁Δt = ρA₂v₂Δt, or A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Therefore Av = constant (6.4). The Equation 6.4 gives equation of continuity, which can be interpreted as the speed of the fluid is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.
Fluid Dynamics
Thus increasing the speed decreases cross-sectional area and vice versa.
Fluid Dynamics

DO YOU KNOW. When water falls from a tap its speed increases under the action of gravity as it comes down; when the speed increases the cross-sectional area decreases to keep the equation of continuity valid.
Fluid Dynamics

Equation 5 can also be written as ΔV/Δt = Av since Av = constant. Therefore ΔV/Δt = constant (6.5). Equation 6.5 shows that the “volume flow rate” (or time rate of flow of volume) is constant. The volume of an incompressible fluid passing through any point in unit time through a pipe of non-uniform cross-section is constant in the steady flow.
Fluid Dynamics

EXAMPLE 6.2 · GARDEN HOSE. A garden hose of inner radius 1.25 cm carries water at 2.60 m/s. The nozzle at the end has radius 0.30 cm. How fast does the water emerge out through the nozzle? GIVEN. Radius of garden hose r₁ = 1.25 cm = 0.0125 m; radius of nozzle r₂ = 0.30 cm = 0.0030 m; speed through garden hose v₁ = 2.60 m/s. REQUIRED. Speed out of nozzle v₂ = ? SOLUTION. The equation of continuity is A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
Fluid Dynamics

The area of circle is A = πr², therefore equation of continuity can also be written as πr₁²v₁ = πr₂²v₂, or r₁²v₁ = r₂²v₂ and v₂ = r₁²v₁/r₂². Putting values: v₂ = ((0.0125 m)² × 2.60 m s⁻¹)/(0.0030 m)² = 45.14 m s⁻¹. Hence, the speed of the water from the nozzle is 45.14 m/s.
Fluid Dynamics

6.5 BERNOULLI’S EQUATION. Bernoulli’s equation relates the pressure, flow speed, and height for flow of an ideal fluid. Mathematically: P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂; P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. Bernoulli’s equation is simply the law of conservation of energy applied to fluids in motion. Consider an ideal flow through a pipe of nonuniform size, as illustrated in Figure 6.8.
Fluid Dynamics

The work W is due to forces other than the conservative force of gravity, so it equals the change in total mechanical energy (kinetic energy plus gravitational potential energy) associated with the fluid element. W = ΔE or W = ΔK + ΔU (1). The total work done will be the sum of all the individual work done: W = W₁ + W₂ (2). For end 1, by definition of work W₁ = F₁·Δx₁ = F₁Δx₁ cosθ; here θ = 0° and cos0° = 1.
Fluid Dynamics
Therefore W₁ = F₁Δx₁ (3).
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.8. A fluid in laminar flow through a constricted pipe. The volume of the shaded section on the left is equal to the volume of the shaded section on the right.
Fluid Dynamics

For end 2, by definition of work W₂ = F₂·Δx₂ = F₂Δx₂ cosθ; here θ = 180° and cos180° = −1. Therefore W₂ = −F₂Δx₂ (4). By definition of pressure P = F/A, or F = PA (5). Putting the value of F from equation 5 in equation 3 and equation 4, we get for end 1 W₁ = P₁A₁Δx₁ (6); for end 2 W₂ = −P₂A₂Δx₂ (7). Since ΔV = AΔx (8), by definition of density ρ = Δm/ΔV or ΔV = Δm/ρ (9).
Fluid Dynamics
Comparing equation 8 and equation 9, Δm/ρ = AΔx (10). Therefore, from equation 10, equations 6 and 7 can be written as for end 1 W₁ = P₁Δm₁/ρ (11); for end 2 W₂ = −P₂Δm₂/ρ (12).
Fluid Dynamics

DO YOU KNOW. Daniel Bernoulli (1700–1782), a Swiss physicist and mathematician, made important discoveries in fluid dynamics. Born into a family of mathematicians, he was the only member of the family to make a mark in physics. Bernoulli’s most famous work, Hydrodynamica, was published in 1738; it is both a theoretical and a practical study of equilibrium, pressure, and speed in fluids.
Fluid Dynamics

He showed that as the speed of a fluid increases, its pressure decreases. In Hydrodynamica Bernoulli also attempted the first explanation of the behavior of gases with changing pressure and temperature; this was the beginning of the kinetic theory of gases.
Fluid Dynamics

Putting values from equations 11 and 12 in equation 2: W = P₁Δm₁/ρ − P₂Δm₂/ρ (13). The net change in kinetic energy ΔK is ΔK = ½Δm₂v₂² − ½Δm₁v₁² (14). The net change in potential energy ΔU is ΔU = Δm₂gh₂ − Δm₁gh₁ (15). Putting values from equation 13, equation 14 and equation 15 in equation 1: P₁Δm₁/ρ − P₂Δm₂/ρ = ½Δm₂v₂² − ½Δm₁v₁² + Δm₂gh₂ − Δm₁gh₁ (16).
Fluid Dynamics

Since for ideal fluid equal mass should flow across both ends, therefore Δm₁ = Δm₂ = Δm (17). From equation 17, equation 16 can be written as P₁Δm/ρ − P₂Δm/ρ = ½Δmv₂² − ½Δmv₁² + Δmgh₂ − Δmgh₁. Taking Δm as common: (Δm/ρ)(P₁−P₂) = Δm(½v₂² − ½v₁² + gh₂ − gh₁). Multiplying both sides by ρ, we get P₁−P₂ = ½ρv₂² − ½ρv₁² + ρgh₂ − ρgh₁.

Therefore P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂ (6.6), or P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant (6.7). Equations 6.6 and 6.7 are termed Bernoulli’s equations. Bernoulli’s equations are based on conservation of energy such that for an incompressible and non-viscous fluid, the total mechanical energy of the fluid is constant.

C. TORRICELLI’S THEOREM (SPEED OF EFFLUX). Torricelli’s theorem states that “the speed of efflux is equal to the speed gained by fluid while falling through height h under the action of gravity.” Consider a large storage tank, which develops a leak at the bottom as shown in Figure 6.11. The pressure at both ends is the same (P₁ = P₂ = P).
Fluid Dynamics

The height h is the difference between the height of the fluid level h₁ and the height of the hole from the ground h₂ (h = h₁ − h₂). Velocity at the top is considered zero (v₁ = 0), while the bottom velocity is to be determined (v₂ = v).
Fluid Dynamics
FIGURE 6.11. A leak at the bottom of a large storage tank.
Fluid Dynamics

By Bernoulli’s equation P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂. Substituting appropriate values and rearranging: P + ½ρ(0)² + ρgh₁ = P + ½ρv² + ρgh₂; or P − P + ρgh₁ − ρgh₂ = ½ρv². Hence ρg(h₁−h₂) = ½ρv², as h₁−h₂ = h. Therefore ρg(h) = ½ρv² or 2gh = v². Taking the square root on both sides, √(v²) = √(2gh); therefore v = √(2gh) (6.7).
Fluid Dynamics

The speed is the same as the vertical velocity which a body gains after falling freely through a height h. Equation 6.7 is termed Torricelli’s equation for the speed of fluid emerging from water storage.

D. VENTURI METRE (FLOW METRE). Venturi metre is a device used to measure the flow speed or flow rate through a piping system. It works on the principle of pressure difference between restricted and unrestricted flow regions. We consider the flow to be steady, and assume the fluid is incompressible and has negligible internal friction. Hence we can use Bernoulli’s equation.
Fluid Dynamics
Consider Figure 6.12; let P₁ and P₂ be the pressure and v₁ and v₂ be the velocities of wide (end 1) and narrow (end 2) sections of the tube respectively.
Fluid Dynamics

FIGURE 6.12. A Venturi tube shows high pressure at the wide section (end 1) and low pressure at the narrow section (end 2); a pressure gauge arrangement illustrates the device. The Bernoulli equation can be written as P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh, or P₁−P₂ = ½ρv₂² − ½ρv₁² (1). By the equation of continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ or v₂ = A₁v₁/A₂ (2). Putting equation 2 in equation 1:
Fluid Dynamics
P₁−P₂ = ½ρ[A₁v₁/A₂]² − ½ρv₁² = ½ρ[(A₁/A₂)²−1]v₁². Rearranging, v₁² = 2(P₁−P₂)/{ρ[(A₁/A₂)²−1]}, and therefore v₁ = A₂√[2(P₁−P₂)/{ρ(A₁²−A₂²)}] (6.8).

This is the solution for speed in a pipe by Venturi’s meter when any barometer (device used to measure pressure) is used. However, when no barometer is used, the height of the fluid in smaller equal-diameter pipes attached to both the pipe and the neck is used as the reference, as shown in Figure 6.13. By the first condition of equilibrium, the pressure difference is related to the height difference.

Putting (P₁−P₂) = ρgh in equation 6.8 gives v₁ = A₂√[2(ρgh)/{ρ(A₁²−A₂²)}]. Therefore v₁ = A₂√[2gh/(A₁²−A₂²)] (6.9).

EXAMPLE 6.5 · AIRCRAFT WING. What is the aerofoil’s lift (in newtons) on a wing of area 88 m² if the air passes at speed 280 m/s over its top surface and at 150 m/s over its bottom surface? GIVEN. Pressure is defined as (P₁−P₂) = F_lift/A or F_lift = (P₁−P₂)×A. By Bernoulli’s equation P₁−P₂ = ½ρ(v₂²−v₁²) + ρgh₂ − ρgh₁. Since h₁ = h₂, P₁−P₂ = ½ρ(v₂²−v₁²). E. BLOOD FLOW. Bernoulli’s equation ignores viscosity (fluid friction). If a fluid had no viscosity, it could flow through a level tube or pipe without a force being applied. Viscosity acts like a sort of friction between fluid layers moving at slightly different speeds. The volume flow rate ΔV/Δt for laminar flow of a viscous fluid through a horizontal, cylindrical pipe depends on its radius.
Fluid Dynamics
A similar case occurs in human arteries. The “blood flow in the human body” depends upon the radius of its arteries, as shown in Figure 6.14.
Fluid Dynamics

FIGURE 6.14. Normal artery; artery narrowed by atherosclerosis, with plaque. If the radius of arteries is reduced as a result of arteriosclerosis (thickening and hardening of artery walls) and cholesterol buildup, the pressure must be increased to maintain the same flow rate.
Fluid Dynamics

If the radius is reduced by half, the heart would have to increase the pressure by a factor of about 2⁴ = 16 to maintain the same blood-flow rate. The heart must work much harder under these conditions, but usually cannot maintain the original flow rate. The pressure is lower where the fluid (blood) is flowing faster. The pressure difference can dislodge the plaque.
Fluid Dynamics
The plaque can then lodge in and block a smaller artery, which can cause heart attack.

When a particle executes repeated movement about a mean position, it is said to be in harmonic motion; if repeated at regular intervals, it is called periodic motion.

Oscillation is a type of harmonic motion, typically periodic, in one or more dimensions. Examples include motion of a spring, a pendulum, or the back-and-forth motion of a swing. 7.2 TERMINOLOGY OF OSCILLATORY MOTION. Figure 7.1(a) shows a simple pendulum. When its bob is displaced to one side and released, it vibrates about its mean position. We use the following terms. (i) VIBRATORY MOTION:

For a pendulum bob, motion from A to B and back from B to A is one vibration, as shown in Figure 7.1(a). (iii) TIME PERIOD: the time required for a body to complete one vibration. (iv) FREQUENCY:
Oscillation
the number of vibrations completed by a body in one second; it is the reciprocal of the time period.

Frequency: f = 1/T. Its unit is hertz: 1 Hz = 1 c s⁻¹ = cps. (v) PERIODIC MOTION: motion repeated in equal intervals of time; for example, motion of the pendulum of a wall clock. (vi) DISPLACEMENT (x): at any instant, the distance of the oscillating body from the mean position. (vii) AMPLITUDE (x₀): the maximum displacement of a body from the mean position. (viii) ANGULAR FREQUENCY (ω):

the number of revolutions per second of a body is called angular frequency; ω = 2πf and f = ω/(2π), where ω is angular velocity. FOR YOUR INFORMATION. Relevant dynamic characteristics of a high-rise building are its natural oscillatory period, mass, stiffness, and damping coefficient.

7.5.1 ENERGY CONSERVATION IN S.H.M. To study energy conservation in simple harmonic motion, consider a mass m suspended from a strong support by a spring of spring constant k as in Figure 7.5. KINETIC ENERGY IN S.H.M. A simple harmonic oscillator moving with instantaneous velocity v has K.E. = ½mv² (1). But v = ω√(x₀²−x²). Putting this value in equation 7.7 gives K.E. = ½mω²(x₀²−x²) = ½k(x₀²−x²) (7.11). K.E. is maximum as the oscillator passes the mean position x = 0: (K.E.)max = ½kx₀² (7.12). For potential energy, the restoring force on the oscillator at displacement x is F_r = −kx = −mω²x (7.14).

Where ω = √(k/m). The force required to displace the mass by x is F = −F_r = −(−mω²x) = mω²x (2). At displacement x the force is mω²x, while at x = 0 the force is zero. Average force during displacement x is F_av = (F_i+F_f)/2 = (0+kx)/2 = ½mω²x (7.15). Work done against restoring force: Work = F_av·x = ½mω²x² (7.16).

By the work-energy principle, this work is stored as elastic potential energy in the oscillating mass-spring system: P.E. = ½mω²x² = ½kx² (7.17). At displacement x, the oscillator’s energy is partly kinetic and partly potential.

Total energy = K.E. + P.E.
