INTRODUCTION. The idea of a wave is useful for a wide range of phenomena and is a basic concept in physics; wave behavior is also important to engineers. A progressive wave is a disturbance moving from its source to surrounding places, transmitting energy from one point to another. Wave motion is the mechanism by which energy is transferred from one point to another.
Waves

Some waves require a medium for propagation, such as sound in air, water waves and waves in a string or spring; these are mechanical waves. Other waves, including heat, light and radio waves, need no medium and are electromagnetic waves. 8.1 PERIODIC WAVES. A source oscillating periodically in a medium produces continuous periodic waves.
Waves

As the source oscillates, it disturbs particles of the medium and sets them vibrating with the same amplitude and frequency, causing wave motion. An example is an ordinary rope fastened at one end to a fixed support, with the other end free as in Figure 8.1.
Waves

If the free end of a rope is moved up and down periodically, a train of transverse waves is produced and moves down the rope. Each portion of the rope moves up and down periodically (Figure 8.1). A more effective periodic oscillating source is an electromagnetic vibrator (Figure 8.2).
Waves

Increasing its frequency produces transverse pulses in the string; the waves travel down the cord from the vibrator to the clamped end. Circular periodic waves can similarly be generated in a ripple tank by spherical dippers just touching the water surface. A small electric motor drives the mechanical arrangement; the dipping rate is controlled by changing motor speed. Figure 8.3 shows the wave pattern at an instant.
Waves
An oscillating mass-spring system is another periodic vibrator: a pen attached to its mass traces a wavy line on paper moving at constant rate.
Waves

Many vibrating objects generate waves. A vibrating object does work on particles of the medium and gives them energy; the particles begin to vibrate, so energy is transmitted from one point to another. Sound waves may originate from a vibrating tuning fork in a laboratory or from a vibrating guitar string. These produce mechanical progressive waves (Figure 8.4). Consider a rope attached at one end to a rigid support.
Waves

A sudden up-and-down movement at the free end sets up a wave that travels along the string at speed v. If the hand continues moving, a series of waves travels along the string. Waves can also be demonstrated by dropping a pebble into a quiet pool: a disturbance at the impact point spreads in all directions over the water surface at the same speed (Figure 8.5).
Waves

To understand how a wave moves along a vibrating cord, consider Figure 8.6: a wave moves to the left along a stretched string as end A makes one complete vibration. (i) At t = 0, A is at the mean position and point B is at a crest. (ii) After t = T/4, A is at the trough while B is at equilibrium; during this time the crest has moved right.
Waves

(iii) After t = T/2, A passes through equilibrium while B is at the trough and the crest has moved further right. (iv) At t = 3T/4, A is at the crest while B is at the mean position and the crest has moved further. (v) After period T, A and B have each completed one oscillation and the crest has moved one wavelength λ.
Waves
The cord particles simply oscillate about their mean positions over a short path, while a wave moves through the medium.
Waves

Particles of the medium oscillate with the same frequency as the wave passing through them. No particle in the disturbance moves far from its initial position; only the disturbance moves through the cord. This is characteristic of wave motion. NECESSARY CONDITIONS FOR WAVE MOTION. Wave propagation occurs through interaction of medium particles, so:
Waves

(i) the medium must be elastic; (ii) its particles must interact and exert forces on one another. Transverse and longitudinal waves can be set up in solids. In fluids, transverse waves die out very quickly and usually cannot be produced. 8.3 CLASSIFICATION OF PROGRESSIVE WAVES. Waves that transmit energy from one place to another are called progressive or traveling waves.
Waves

They are classified as (a) transverse and (b) longitudinal waves. 8.3.1 TRANSVERSE WAVES. In transverse waves, particles of the medium vibrate along a line perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. When a disturbance propagates through a medium, its particles are disturbed and start vibrating. If particle vibration is perpendicular to wave propagation, it is a transverse wave pulse.
Waves
The particles vibrate with the source’s period and frequency. WAVE CREST. The portion of a wave above the mean level is a wave crest.
Waves

WAVE TROUGH. The portion of a wave below the mean level is a wave trough. EXAMPLES. If one end of a string is attached to a strong support and the other end is free, periodically moving the free end up and down produces transverse waves (Figure 8.7). Each cord particle vibrates perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
Waves

When a pebble is dropped into a quiet pond, a circular pattern spreads from the impact point (Figure 8.8). To investigate whether water molecules at the surface move as a wave passes, drop a piece of paper on the surface and watch it move. A piece of cork does not travel along with the wave.
Waves
In transverse waves, medium particles vibrate along a line at right angles to propagation; thus water waves are transverse waves.
Waves

Light, radio, television and mobile-phone signals are transverse electromagnetic waves and can travel through a vacuum. Mechanical waves can be set up in solids and on liquid surfaces, where particles are close enough to exert large forces on one another. In gases, molecules are far apart and act independently, so mechanical transverse waves cannot propagate through gases. 8.3.2 LONGITUDINAL OR COMPRESSIONAL WAVES.
Waves

Longitudinal waves consist of compressions and rarefactions. A region where particles are crowded is a compression; where particles are least crowded is a rarefaction. In longitudinal waves, medium particles vibrate about their mean positions along the direction of wave propagation. Example: a slinky spring.
Waves

When a stretched slinky spring is pushed forward, loops near the applied force are compressed before the disturbance reaches the rest of the spring. Compressed loops exert force on loops to their right, so a compressional pulse travels along the spring.
Waves

When the spring is pulled backward, loops near the applied force are rarefacted first; these exert force on loops to their right and a rarefaction travels along the spring. Pushing and pulling the spring at a constant rate sets up longitudinal waves. Other examples are sound waves and shock waves produced during an earthquake, also called seismic waves (Figure 8.10). 8.3.3 CHARACTERISTICS OF A WAVE.
Waves

A wave is specified by wave speed, frequency, time period, phase, wavelength, amplitude and intensity. WAVE SPEED. The speed of a wave is the distance it travels per unit time. It depends on the type of wave and the properties of the medium.
Waves

For a transverse wave pulse in an elastic stretched string or spring, v = √(T L/M) (8.1), where M is the string mass, L its length and T the tension. If μ is the string mass per unit length, v = √(T/μ) (8.2). Thus a well-stretched, thin string has a greater transverse-wave speed than a loose, thick one. The speed of a compressional or longitudinal wave depends on the medium’s elastic modulus E and density ρ:
Waves

v = √(E/ρ) (8.3). Longitudinal waves travel more slowly in gases than in solids because gases are more compressible and have a smaller elastic modulus E. FREQUENCY OF WAVE. The number of waves passing a point per unit time is the wave frequency.
Waves

As a wave progresses, each medium particle oscillates with the frequency and period of the source; wave frequency f equals the frequency of the simple harmonic oscillating source. Frequency = number of waves passing a point / time taken. TIME PERIOD OF WAVE. As a wave progresses, its particles vibrate with the source’s period; the wave period equals the period of the simple harmonic oscillator.
Waves
The time during which a wave passes a certain point is its time period; it equals the reciprocal of frequency: T = 1/f.
Waves

WAVELENGTH λ. The distance between two successive particles exactly in the same state of vibration is the wavelength λ. In Figure 8.11, A and C, P and Q, or B and D are in the same phase because they have the same state of vibration. One wavelength is emitted as the wave source completes one vibration. During time period T, the wave travels distance λ, so v = distance/time = λ/T = fλ (8.4).
Waves

This relation is true for all waves. AMPLITUDE OF WAVE. The maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its equilibrium position on either side is the amplitude, indicated by y₀. INTENSITY OF WAVE. Energy transmitted per second per unit area placed perpendicular to wave propagation is wave intensity, indicated by I. EXAMPLE 8.1 · A WAVE GENERATOR. A wave generator produces 500 pulses in 10 s.
Waves
Find the period and frequency.
Waves

EXAMPLE 8.1 SOLUTION. GIVEN: 500 pulses in 10 s. Required: (a) period T; (b) frequency f. (a) T = 10/500 = 1/50 s. (b) f = 1/T = 50 pulses s⁻¹. Answer: T = 1/50 s, f = 50 pulses s⁻¹. POINT TO PONDER. Sun explosions occur at the Sun’s surface due to fission and fusion reactions, but we cannot hear them. Why? EXAMPLE 8.2 · RIPPLE TANK. In a ripple tank, 40 waves pass a point in one second.
Waves
If wavelength is 5 cm, find wave speed. GIVEN: f = 40 waves s⁻¹; λ = 5 cm. Required: v. Formula v = fλ. Therefore v = 40 waves s⁻¹ × 5 cm = 200 cm s⁻¹ = 2 m s⁻¹. Answer: v = 2 m s⁻¹.
Waves

8.4 SPEED OF SOUND. Distance covered by a sound wave per unit time is its speed. Sound waves are compressional. The speed of a mechanical wave in a medium depends on (i) density and (ii) elasticity of the medium. Newton derived the expression: speed = √(elastic modulus of medium / density of medium), or v = √(E/ρ) (8.5).
Waves

Newton assumed sound travels through air and other gases under isothermal conditions, meaning no temperature change as sound waves travel. Under this condition the elastic modulus equals gas pressure, as follows. Let V be air volume at pressure p. Increase pressure from p to p + Δp and reduce volume from V to V − ΔV at constant temperature. Boyle’s law gives pV = (p + Δp)(V − ΔV), hence pΔV = ΔpV − ΔpΔV.
Waves
For small pressure and volume changes, neglect ΔpΔV, so pΔV = ΔpV. Therefore p = ΔpV/ΔV = Δp/(ΔV/V) = stress/volumetric strain = E.
Waves

Newton’s formula for the speed of sound in air or a gas follows from v = √(p/ρ) (8.6). Since p = ρₘgh, (8.7), where ρₘ is the density of mercury at S.T.P., ρₘ = 13.6 g cm⁻³, g = 980 cm s⁻², h = 76 cm, and air density ρ = 0.001293 g cm⁻³, the book calculates v = √[(13.6 × 980 × 76)/0.001293] = 281 m s⁻¹. The experimental speed of sound in gas is 332 m s⁻¹; thus this theoretical value is 16% lower.
Waves
8.4.1 LAPLACE’S CORRECTION. This section begins by introducing the difference between theoretical and experimental speeds of sound in gas.
Waves

Rapid changes in air pressure, volume and temperature occur under adiabatic conditions. For an adiabatic process, PVᵞ = constant (8.8), where P is pressure, V is gas volume and γ is a constant depending on the gas. Increase pressure from P to P + ΔP and decrease volume from V to V − ΔV. Then PVᵞ = (P + ΔP)(V − ΔV)ᵞ = (P + ΔP)Vᵞ(1 − ΔV/V)ᵞ.
Waves

Applying the binomial theorem and neglecting square and higher powers of ΔV/V gives P = (P + ΔP)(1 − γΔV/V). Expanding gives P = P − γPΔV/V + ΔP − γΔPΔV/V. Neglect the term γΔPΔV/V; therefore γPΔV/V = ΔP, and γP = ΔP/(ΔV/V) = stress/volumetric strain.
Waves

The corrected elastic modulus for the isothermal process is γP = E. The speed of sound in air or gas becomes v = √(γP/ρ) (8.9), or v = √(γρₘgh/ρ) (8.10). For air, γ = 1.42; using mercury density at S.T.P. ρₘ = 13.6 g cm⁻³, g = 980 cm s⁻², h = 76 cm, and air density ρ = 0.001293 g cm⁻³, the book calculates v = 33310 cm s⁻¹ = 333 m s⁻¹.
Waves

This agrees reasonably with experimental value 332 m s⁻¹, so the Laplace correction is supported. 8.4.2 EFFECTS OF VARIOUS FACTORS ON SPEED OF SOUND IN AIR. Sound waves are compressional mechanical waves in gas/air with speed v = √(γP/ρ). (1) Density: speed varies inversely with the square root of gas density. (2) Moisture:
Waves

moisture reduces air’s resultant density, so speed increases with humidity; sound travels faster in damp than dry air. (3) Pressure: for one mole of an ideal gas of volume V and pressure P at temperature T, PV = RT (8.11). R is the general gas constant. If gas mass is m, its density is ρ = m/V.
Waves

From PV = RT, V = RT/P (8.11). For gas mass m, density is ρ = m/V (8.12). Therefore sound speed is v = √(γRT/m) (8.13), and is independent of gas pressure. TEMPERATURE. For solids and liquids, the change in sound speed with temperature is very small and may be neglected. For gases it is large: speed increases about 0.6 m s⁻¹ per 1°C rise.
Waves

Since v depends on the square root of the gas’s absolute temperature, if v₀ and v are sound speeds at temperatures T₀ and T, then v/v₀ = √(T/T₀) (8.14). For 0°C, T₀ = (0 + 273) K and for t°C, T = (t + 273) K. Applying the binomial theorem and neglecting higher powers gives √[(t + 273)/273] ≈ 1 + t/546 (8.15). Since at 0°C, v₀ = 332 m s⁻¹, v = 332(1 + t/546) = 332 + 0.61t m s⁻¹ (8.16).
Waves
The increase per degree is approximately 0.61 m s⁻¹.
Waves

EXAMPLE 8.3 · STEEL RAILWAY TRACK. Find the speed of sound in a steel railway track if steel density is 7800 kg m⁻³ and elastic modulus is 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻². GIVEN: ρ = 7800 kg m⁻³; E = 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻². REQUIRED: sound speed v. Formula v = √(E/ρ). Substitution: v = √[(2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻²)/(7800 kg m⁻³)] = 5.06 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Answer: 5.06 × 10³ m s⁻¹. ASSIGNMENT 8.1 · SEA WATER.
Waves
The visible start gives the speed of sound in sea water; the given elastic modulus is 2.1 × 10⁹ N m⁻², and the printed answer is (1430 m s⁻¹).
Waves

EXAMPLE 8.4 · NEON GAS. Find sound speed in neon at 0°C (molar mass 20.18 g mol⁻¹; γ = 1.66 for a monoatomic gas). GIVEN: T = 273 K; molar mass m = 20.18 g mol⁻¹ = 0.02018 kg mol⁻¹; γ = 1.66; R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Sound speed v = √(γRT/m) = √[(1.66 × 8.314 × 273)/0.02018] = 432 m s⁻¹. Answer: 432 m s⁻¹. 8.5 SUPERPOSITION OF WAVES. When two transverse pulses on a long narrow spring approach and cross, they superpose.
Waves

The resultant displacement at a point equals the sum of displacements caused by each pulse there. After crossing, each pulse continues with its original shape and speed as if nothing happened. Two equal, opposite pulses cancel when they meet and net spring displacement is zero. Unlike particles, waves pass through one another unaffected. The principle of superposition is introduced.
Waves

When two or more waves pass through the same region at the same time, total displacement at an interaction point equals the vector sum of individual displacements. If n waves displace a particle by y₁, y₂, …, yₙ, the resultant is y = y₁ + y₂ + … + yₙ (8.17). This is the principle of superposition. 8.6 INTERFERENCE OF WAVES.
Waves

The effect produced by superposition of waves from two coherent sources passing through the same region is interference. Sources are coherent if their phase difference is constant; they have the same frequency and amplitude. Where wave trains from coherent sources meet, superposition reinforces waves at some points and cancels them at others.
Waves
Figure 8.12 illustrates constructive interference of equal in-phase pulses; Figure 8.13 illustrates destructive interference of equal out-of-phase pulses.
Waves

The resulting effect is an interference pattern. Coherent sources have constant phase difference, so they must have the same frequency and amplitude. There are two types. (i) CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE. When two waves arrive at the same place at the same time in phase, they reinforce. Resultant displacement at the superposition point equals the vector sum of individual displacements.
Waves

For transverse waves, a crest meets a crest and a trough meets a trough. The figure gives PS = QS + RS and BC = BD − AB. For longitudinal waves, compression meets compression and rarefaction meets rarefaction. (ii) DESTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE. If two waves arrive at the same place at the same time out of phase by 180°, destructive interference occurs.
Waves
The resultant amplitude equals the difference between individual amplitudes: y = y₁ − y₂.
Waves

In sound waves (compressional waves), destructive interference occurs when a compression meets a rarefaction. 8.6.1 CONDITIONS FOR INTERFERENCE. For constructive or destructive interference: (i) the waves must be phase-coherent; (ii) they must arrive at the same place at the same time; (iii) they must travel in the same direction; (iv) linear superposition must hold.
Waves

(a) Constructive interference requires waves in phase; path difference is zero or an integral multiple of wavelength: d = 0, λ, 2λ, 3λ, …; d = mλ. (b) Destructive interference requires waves 180° out of phase; d = (m + ½)λ, where m = 0, 1, 2, … . 8.7 INTERFERENCE OF SOUND WAVES. When two coherent waves arrive together at the same place they reinforce and interfere.
Waves

The phenomenon can be demonstrated with a vibrating tuning fork held above a tube. Sound entering the tube splits into two parts: half the intensity travels along path ACB to point B and the other half along ADB. The waves reunite at B, where an ear or other detector can detect them. If paths ACB and ADB are equal, they arrive in phase, causing constructive interference and loud sound.
Waves

In the sound-interference apparatus, drawing out the sliding tube makes path ADB longer than ACB. If the path difference is half a wavelength, the waves interfere destructively and no sound is heard at B. Pinching the rubber tube at C stops waves along that path, and the ear hears sound again; this shows the silence was due to destructive interference. 8.8 BEATS.
Waves

We discussed superposition of two sound waves with the same frequency. If two slightly different frequencies are superposed, a stationary observer detects fluctuating loudness: loud, faint, loud, faint. This periodic variation in loudness heard when two notes of slightly different frequencies are played simultaneously is called beats.
Waves

Two sources with slightly different frequencies produce a single note whose intensity rises and falls. To study beats, take two audio-frequency generators, such as 256 Hz tuning forks; add a little wax to fork B so its frequency becomes 254 Hz; place both equally distant from the ear and sound them together. At t₁ = 0, both forks are in phase and send compressions toward the ear, so loud sound is heard.
Waves

As time passes, fork B has slightly lower frequency than A and falls behind. After t₂ = 1/4 s, fork A completes 64 vibrations and sends a compression, while fork B completes 63½ vibrations and sends a rarefaction; compression and rarefaction cancel at the ear, so no sound is heard. At t₃ = 1/2 s both send compressions together and loud sound returns.
Waves

At t₄ = 3/4 s, A sends a compression while B sends a rarefaction; they cancel and sound is faint. At t₅ = 1 s, A completes 256 vibrations and B 254; both send compressions together and loud sound returns. Thus two beats per second are produced, equal to the difference between fork frequencies. Number of beats per second N = f₁ − f₂ (8.17). Figure 8.17 depicts the two tuning forks at successive times.
Waves

When two waves travel along the same line simultaneously, the resultant displacement of a particle is the vector sum of the displacements due to each wave. Their resultant wave amplitude varies with time, causing loudness variation called beats. BEAT FREQUENCY. The difference between the frequencies of two waves is beat frequency N. The interval between successive loud sounds is beat period T.
Waves

During T, the waves complete f₁T and f₂T oscillations, differing by one: f₁T − f₂T = 1. Therefore N = f₁ − f₂ = 1/T (8.19), where f₁ − f₂ is beat frequency and T is beat period. Beats are used to find unknown frequencies and tune musical instruments. Tuning adjusts the pitch of one or more tones until they form the desired arrangement. Pitch is the perceived fundamental frequency of sound.
Waves
Instruments produce vibrations and their sound waves are measured in hertz.
Waves

TUNING MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS. Tuning is performed by sounding two pitches and adjusting one to match or relate to the other. Tuning forks, pianos and other devices can provide a reference pitch. If two played pitches have different frequencies they produce a beating sound called “interference beats.” As two notes approach a harmonic relationship, beat frequency decreases.
Waves

Adjust the instrument until beating slows so much it cannot be detected. EXAMPLE 8.5. Two pianos sound the same note. One vibrates at 221.60 Hz and the other at 221.40 Hz. Find beat frequency. GIVEN: f₁ = 221.60 Hz; f₂ = 221.40 Hz. Beat frequency f = f₁ − f₂ = 0.20 Hz. Answer: 0.20 Hz. ASSIGNMENT 8.2. How many beats per second are heard when tuning forks of 256 Hz and 259 Hz sound together?
Waves

8.9 REFLECTION OF WAVES AND PHASE CHANGE. The bouncing back of waves from a medium boundary is reflection. MECHANICAL WAVES. The behavior of a mechanical wave at a boundary can be studied with pulses along a narrow spring or string. The page begins the case of an upward transverse pulse traveling toward a fixed wall; part of its energy is absorbed and the rest reflected.
Waves

For a wave reflected at a fixed end, an upward displacement pulse returns downward: the incident and reflected pulses have a 180° or π-radian phase change, equivalent to half a wavelength (λ/2). If the string end is attached to a ring that moves freely up and down, an arriving pulse lifts the ring and its return produces an upward pulse; there is no phase change.
Waves

Thus, reflection from a denser medium causes a 180° (π rad) phase change, while reflection at the boundary of a rarer medium causes no phase change. The same principle applies to longitudinal waves. ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES. A phase change also occurs when electromagnetic waves such as light reflect from a denser medium.
Waves

Radar (radio detection and ranging) waves locate objects by reflecting waves of known speed from them. REFLECTION OF SOUND WAVES. Sound waves obey the laws of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Waves

Regular reflection of sound occurs when the reflecting surface treats all parts of the incident wavefront similarly; it must be flat to within a fraction of the wavelength. Sound waves above 20 kHz are used to determine shoals of fish in the ocean. A ship sends an underwater sound pulse; after reflection from the sea bottom, an underwater receiver detects it and records the time interval.
Waves

Submarines are also detected by underwater sound waves from their propellers. ECHO. Reflection of an original sound from an object received 0.1 s later than direct sound is an echo. At sound speed about 340 m s⁻¹, effective distance to the reflector is (340 × 0.1)/2 = 17 m. Echoes in halls and auditoriums can be reduced by choosing suitable dimensions and avoiding continuous flat smooth walls. REVERBERATION.
Waves

If the reflecting surface is less than 17 m from the source, echo follows the direct sound too closely to distinguish; this is reverberation, which confuses the sound impression. 8.10 STATIONARY WAVES. Sound from most string and wind instruments is due to stationary or standing waves. Vibrating strings of guitars and pianos set up stationary waves of definite frequencies.
Waves

The source asks how stationary waves differ from progressive waves and how they are produced. Stationary waves can form in a medium but do not transmit energy from place to place as progressive waves do.
Waves

A stationary or standing wave forms when two plane waves of the same amplitude and frequency travel at the same speed in opposite directions and superpose. ACTIVITY. Tie one end of a rubber cord to a strong support and wiggle the other at frequency f₁. Transverse waves travel along the rope from the hand; at the fixed end they reflect with a slightly different shape.
Waves

They superpose with newly generated waves, producing a stationary wave in which the cord vibrates in one loop. Its form does not move in either direction of the incident or reflected waves, hence “stationary.” Points that do not vibrate are nodes N. Midpoints between successive nodes, where amplitude is maximum, are antinodes A. Distance between successive nodes or antinodes is λ/2; adjacent node to antinode is λ/4.
Waves

If frequency is increased to twice the initial frequency, f₂ = 2f₁, a stationary wave forms with two loops; this is the second harmonic. Similarly, 3f₁, 4f₁, …, nf₁ produce the third, fourth, …, nth harmonics with 3, 4, …, n loops.
Waves

To demonstrate mechanical transverse stationary waves, consider a string of length L stretched by clamping both ends so tension is T. Pluck the string at different positions to find its characteristic frequencies. Plucking the midpoint sends transverse waves toward both ends. They reflect at the clamped ends, meet again at the middle and superpose to form a stationary wave.
Waves

The whole string vibrates in one loop with nodes at its fixed ends and an antinode at the middle (Figure 8.24). The stationary-wave frequency equals the frequency f₁ of each progressive wave. The distance between successive nodes is half a wavelength, so L = λ₁/2 and λ₁ = 2L. Therefore f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/(2L) (8.20).
Waves
If M is total string mass, progressive-wave speed is v = √(TL/M), where T is string tension and L its length. Thus f₁ = (1/2L)√(TL/M).
Waves

With mass per unit length μ = M/L, the fundamental frequency becomes f₁ = (1/2L)√(T/μ) (8.21). This is the characteristic vibration frequency called the fundamental or first harmonic. If a string of length L and linear density μ is plucked at one quarter of its length, it vibrates in two loops (Figure 8.25).
Waves

For wavelength λ₂, L = 2(λ₂/2), so λ₂ = L and f₂ = v/λ₂ = v/L = 2f₁ (8.22); the two-loop frequency is double the fundamental. If the same string is plucked at one sixth of its length, it vibrates in three segments (Figure 8.26). For this mode L = 3(λ₃/2), so λ₃ = 2L/3. The frequency is f₃ = v/λ₃ = 3v/(2L) = 3f₁ (8.23).
Waves

For a string plucked at an arbitrary point, it may resonate in n loops with (n + 1) nodes and n antinodes. Wavelength λₙ = 2L/n (8.24) and frequency fₙ = nf₁ = (n/2L)√(T/μ) (8.25). CONCLUSIONS. (i) A string resonates in whole segments, each segment being the distance between adjacent nodes. A string firmly fixed at both ends resonates only when its length is a whole-number multiple of half-wavelength:
Waves

λ/2, 2λ/2, 3λ/2, … . (ii) As the number of loops increases, frequency increases and wavelength decreases correspondingly; their product remains equal to wave speed. 8.12 FUNDAMENTAL AND OVERTONE VIBRATIONS. A string fixed at both ends resonates only at particular frequencies f₁, f₂, …, fₙ. The lowest characteristic vibration frequency f₁ is the fundamental or first harmonic.
Waves
Other vibration modes whose frequencies are integral multiples of the lowest frequency are overtones or harmonics.
Waves

RESONANCE OF A STRETCHED STRING. When a stretched string is driven by a small periodic force at one of its quantized frequencies, resonance produces a stationary wave. Only the discrete frequencies f₁, f₂, f₃, … are possible; the resonant frequencies are quantized and separated by frequency gaps. EXAMPLE 8.6. A wave speed on a string is 24 m s⁻¹ and the string is 6.0 m long.
Waves

At what driving frequencies will it resonate? Possible wavelengths λₙ = 2L/n: λ₁ = 12 m, λ₂ = 6 m, λ₃ = 4 m. Corresponding frequencies are 24/12 = 2 Hz, 24/6 = 4 Hz and 24/4 = 6 Hz. Answer: 2 Hz, 4 Hz and 6 Hz. EXAMPLE 8.7. A 4.0 m string has mass 3.0 g, one end fixed and the other passing over a pulley carrying a 20 kg mass. Find transverse-wave speed. GIVEN:
Waves

L = 4.0 m; string mass = 0.003 kg; hanging mass M = 20 kg. Mass per unit length μ = 0.003/4.0 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. Tension T = Mg = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N. Therefore v = √(T/μ) = 511.2 m s⁻¹. ASSIGNMENT 8.3. A 40 g string 2 m long vibrates in three loops under tension 270 N. Find wavelength and frequency. (1.33 m, 87.1 Hz.) 8.13 RESONANCE OF AIR COLUMNS AND ORGAN PIPES.
Waves

Stationary waves with discrete frequencies can form in any medium, including air columns as well as stretched strings, springs and elastic membranes. Holding a sounding tuning fork over the open end of a glass tube filled with water can greatly amplify the sound under certain conditions.
Waves
Slowly lower the water surface using a reservoir; at a certain water height, the air column resonates loudly with the tuning-fork sound (Figure 8.27).
Waves

Stationary waves with a discrete set of frequencies can form in an air column, as in a stretched string, spring or elastic membrane. A sounding tuning fork held above the open end of a glass tube filled with water can produce greatly amplified sound under suitable conditions. Slowly lower the water surface in the tube with a reservoir.
Waves
At a certain water height, the air column resonates loudly with the tuning-fork sound (Figure 8.27). The figure labels the fundamental tone and first overtone modes.
Waves

Resonance occurs when tuning-fork frequency fₑ equals the air-column fundamental frequency f₀; several tube heights usually resonate. Stationary longitudinal waves in pipes are the sound source in wind instruments such as flute, organ, trombone and clarinet (Figure 8.28). ORGAN PIPES. An organ pipe produces sound through a vibrating air column. There are two types: closed and open organ pipes.
Waves

In each, air is set vibrating by blowing into the whistle end. CLOSED ORGAN PIPE. A pipe closed opposite the whistle end is a closed organ pipe. Its air column is vibrated by sending a narrow air jet toward the lip at the open end. Air striking the lip sends a compression into the pipe; it reflects from the closed end toward the open end.
Waves
At the lip, this compression pushes the air stream outside, sending a rarefaction into the pipe.
Waves

The rarefaction reflects from the closed end and returns to the lip, drawing the air stream into the pipe and producing a new compression. This sets the air column into vigorous, large-amplitude vibration and creates a stationary wave. A node forms at the closed end; an antinode forms at the open end because air molecules move freely there (Figure 8.29). (a) FIRST HARMONIC.
Waves

For pipe length L and sound wavelength λ₁, L = λ₁/4, so λ₁ = 4L and f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/(4L). This is the fundamental or first harmonic. (b) THIRD HARMONIC. For the third harmonic, L = 3λ₃/4, λ₃ = 4L/3 and f₃ = v/λ₃ = 3v/(4L) = 3f₁. (c) FIFTH HARMONIC. For the fifth harmonic, L = 5λ₅/4 and f₅ = 5v/(4L) = 5f₁.
Waves
Thus a closed pipe supports frequencies fₙ = nv/(4L) for odd n = 1, 3, 5, …; f₁ is the fundamental and higher odd multiples are harmonics.
Waves

For the closed organ pipe, the third harmonic frequency is f₃ = 3v/(4L) = 3f₁; for the fifth harmonic f₅ = 5v/(4L) = 5f₁. Possible frequencies are v/(4L), 3v/(4L), 5v/(4L), …, (2n−1)v/(4L), where n = 1, 2, 3, … . The lowest frequency v/(4L) is the fundamental; higher odd multiples are harmonics. OPEN ORGAN PIPE. A pipe whose end opposite the blowing end is open is an open organ pipe.
Waves
Both ends are open, so both have antinodes and there is a node in the middle. (a) FUNDAMENTAL FREQUENCY. For length L, L = λ₁/2, so λ₁ = 2L and f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/(2L).
Waves

For the open pipe fundamental, λ₁ = 2L and f₁ = v/(2L). (b) SECOND HARMONIC / FIRST OVERTONE. L = 2(λ₂/2) = λ₂, so λ₂ = L and f₂ = v/λ₂ = 2(v/2L) = 2f₁. (c) THIRD HARMONIC / SECOND OVERTONE. The wavelength is λ₃ = 2L/3 and f₃ = v/λ₃ = 3(v/2L) = 3f₁. In general, for the nth harmonic λₙ = 2L/n and fₙ = nv/(2L) = nf₁ (8.26). The figures show the fundamental, first overtone and second overtone modes.
Waves

The lowest frequency v/(2L) is the fundamental or first harmonic; higher integral multiples are the second, third, … harmonics. ACTIVITY. Blow softly across a soft-drink bottle opening. The sound wave reflected from the bottom interferes with the incoming wave to produce a standing wave. Since the bottle is closed at one end, there is a displacement node at the bottom.
Waves

Add varying amounts of water and listen for other resonances. Resonant sound is noticeably louder than non-resonant sound; the longer the air column, the lower the pitch. EXAMPLE 8.9 · OPEN PIPE. A pipe open at one end and closed at the other is 82 cm long. Find its three lowest resonant frequencies; sound speed is 340 m s⁻¹. L = 82 cm = 0.82 m. For lowest frequency λ₁ = 4L and f₁ = v/(4L) = 340/(4 × 0.82) = 104 Hz.
Waves

As in a closed pipe, only odd harmonics are present: f₂ = 3f₁ = 312 Hz; f₃ = 5f₁ = 520 Hz. Answer: 104 Hz, 312 Hz and 520 Hz. ASSIGNMENT 8.5. What length closed pipe produces fundamental frequency 256 Hz at 20°C? (33.5 cm.) 8.14 DOPPLER EFFECT. The apparent change in sound frequency caused by relative motion of the source, listener or both is the Doppler effect.
Waves

It relates measured wave frequency to the relative velocity of source and receiver. Christian Johann Doppler showed in 1842 that relative motion between source and observer shifts frequencies of sound and light. A source S emits sound waves of speed v, frequency f and wavelength λ. If S and listener A are at rest, the listener receives f waves per second.
Waves
Since f waves occupy distance v, wavelength λ = v/f, so f = v/λ. 8.15.1 SOURCE MOVING, LISTENER AT REST. The source may move toward or away from a stationary listener.
Waves

(I-A) SOURCE MOVES TOWARD A STATIONARY LISTENER. A source S moves at speed a toward stationary listener L. The first wave travels distance v in one second and reaches L. In the same second the source moves distance a and emits its last wave. Thus f waves are compressed into distance (v − a); apparent wavelength λ′ = (v − a)/f. The changed frequency is f′ = v/λ′, hence f′ = [v/(v − a)]f (8.27).
Waves

If the source approaches a stationary listener, sound frequency and pitch increase. (I-B) SOURCE MOVES AWAY FROM A STATIONARY LISTENER. 8.16 ULTRASONIC WAVES. A normal human ear hears frequencies from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz cannot be heard. An ultrasonic device can vibrate at 25 billion Hz. An ultrasonic wave is a pressure wave with extremely short wavelength because of its high frequency. Physical Optics

Interference and diffraction are most easily understood by treating light as a wave. Interference occurs when two or more light sources are superimposed. Diffraction occurs when part of a wavefront is obstructed, for example by a narrow slit. Diffraction is first treated qualitatively, before a quantitative treatment of two-slit interference and its extension to transmission through a diffraction grating.
Physical Optics
Polarization establishes the transverse nature of light and has applications discussed in this unit.
Physical Optics

FOR YOUR INFORMATION. Study of the properties and nature of light has been active since Ibn al-Haytham’s time (945 A.D.). The source calls him “Alhozen”; he scientifically studied reflection and refraction, discovered the laws of reflection and recognized a relation between angles of incidence and refraction, though he could not discover their relation. 9.1 NATURE OF LIGHT.
Physical Optics

An important development was Maxwell’s work: in 1873 he showed that light is high-frequency electromagnetic waves. The electric and magnetic field vectors oscillate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
Physical Optics

Maxwell’s theory predicts electromagnetic waves travel at about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and require no medium. Presently we believe light has a dual nature: in reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference and polarization, light behaves like a wave; in the photoelectric effect and Compton shift, it behaves like a particle. Figure 9.1: Electromagnetic waves.
Physical Optics

9.2 WAVEFRONT. As a wave passes through a medium, its particles are disturbed and execute simple harmonic motion. When a small stone falls into still pond water, circular crests move outward from the impact point (Figure 9.2). All points on a crest have the same vibration state and phase. A wavefront is the locus of all points in a medium having the same phase.
Physical Optics

A point source S emits waves in every direction at speed c. In three-dimensional space, a point source in a homogeneous medium has concentric spherical wavefronts centered at S. A portion of a spherical wave is called a circular wavefront. The waves travel outward; arrows from the source show the propagation direction.
Physical Optics

The arrows indicating wavefront propagation are called rays. Rays are always perpendicular to wavefronts (Figure 9.3), so wave motion can be specified by rays or by drawing the wave itself. Illuminance varies inversely with the square of distance from a light source (Figure 9.3). As a wave travels from its source, its curvature decreases.
Physical Optics
At a very large distance, a small portion of a spherical wavefront becomes nearly plane; this straight portion is called a plane wavefront.
Physical Optics

9.3 HUYGENS’ PRINCIPLE. Knowing the shape and location of a wavefront at time t enables determination of the new wavefront’s shape and location at t + Δt. The principle has two parts: (1) Every point on a wavefront may be treated as a source of secondary spherical wavelets. They spread in the forward direction at the wave’s propagation speed.
Physical Optics
(2) The new wavefront at time t + Δt is the plane surface tangent to all secondary wavelets. Figure 9.4 shows the construction for spherical and plane wavefronts; wavelets expand a distance cΔt.
Physical Optics

Figure 9.4 construction: AB is a spherical wavefront at time t from source S. To find its position and shape at t + Δt, take points 1–10 on AB as sources of secondary wavelets. These are hemispheres of radius cΔt, where c is the speed of light. A′B′ is drawn tangent to the wavelets and is the new wavefront after Δt.
Physical Optics

The first phrase specifying how A′B′ is drawn is clipped at the source’s right edge [source text clipped]. Similarly, a plane wavefront’s later position is found using Huygens’ principle (Figure 9.4b).
Physical Optics

9.4 COHERENT SOURCES. The source defines sources producing waves of the same frequency, “eq[clipped] comparable amplitude,” and constant phase difference as “co[clipped] sources.” Our most important source of light and life-sustaining radiation is the Sun. The source says most artificial light sources are hot bodies radiating visible and infrared radiation.
Physical Optics

Each source emits a very large number of waves with random phases. Light is emitted in short bursts when electrons in individual atoms undergo energy changes very quickly and randomly; phase changes abruptly as different atoms act. This is true for light from different parts of the same source except a laser.
Physical Optics
The sentence introducing two methods for obtaining coherent waves from a point source is cut off at the page edge [source continuation clipped].
Physical Optics

Methods to obtain coherent light include (i) division of wavelength, as in Young’s double slits, Fresnel’s biprism and Lloyd’s mirror; and (ii) division of amplitude by partial reflection and transmission at a boundary, as in Newton’s rings. DO YOU KNOW? Monochromatic (single-colour) light has a single wavelength.
Physical Optics
A truly monochromatic source is difficult to obtain, but filters can provide light within a narrow wavelength band.
Physical Optics

9.5 INTERFERENCE OF LIGHT. Interference is the effect produced by superposition of waves from two coherent sources passing through the same region. When two light waves of the same frequency and amplitude, with a constant phase relationship, travel in the same direction, they reinforce at some points and cancel at others. This superposition phenomenon is called interference of light.
Physical Optics
Before Thomas Young, scientists had not successfully demonstrated light interference because their sources were not coherent.
Physical Optics

CONDITIONS TO OBSERVE INTERFERENCE OF LIGHT: (i) Light waves must come from two coherent sources. (ii) Their amplitudes must be equal or nearly equal. (iii) They should be perfectly monochromatic. (iv) The path difference between waves from the sources must be small. (v) Linear superposition must apply.
Physical Optics
To observe interference, place a screen some distance from the two coherent light sources, as shown in Figure 9.5 (continued).
Physical Optics

Two coherent monochromatic light waves from the two sources interfere constructively at some screen points and destructively at others, producing bright and dark fringes (Figure 9.5). CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE. Where coherent light waves meet in phase and reinforce, constructive interference occurs and brightness is observed. Figure 9.6: Waves y₁ and y₂ add to produce a larger-amplitude resultant y.
Physical Optics

At points where phase difference is 0, 2π, 4π, …, the source text gives corresponding path differences 0, λ, 2λ, 3λ, …; constructive interference occurs. Thus the condition in terms of path difference is d = mλ (9.1), where m = 0, 1, 2, 3, … .
Physical Optics

DESTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE. When two wave trains meet in opposite phase, they cancel and dark fringes appear on the screen (Figure 9.7). Phase differences π, 3π, 5π, 7π, … correspond respectively to path differences λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, 7λ/2, … . Thus destructive interference occurs when d = (m + 1/2)λ (9.2), where m = 0, 1, 2, … . Figure 9.7: Two waves cancel each other.
Physical Optics

For two wave trains reaching one point along different paths, they must come from the same source. Any phase change in the source then occurs in both wave trains, and stationary interference effects result. FOR YOUR INFORMATION — TELEVISION PICTURE DISTORTION. A low-flying aircraft can reflect waves from a transmitting antenna toward a receiving aerial. The direct and reflected waves interfere.
Physical Optics
The reflected wave is usually weaker, so interference is not completely destructive; this causes distortion on the television screen.
Physical Optics

9.6 YOUNG’S DOUBLE SLITS EXPERIMENT. In 1801, Thomas Young performed his famous double-slit experiment, providing experimental evidence for the wave theory of light. The principle is division of a wavefront. To obtain phase coherence between interfering light beams, Young split the wavefront of the same monochromatic light into two parts and allowed them to interfere. Figure 9.8:
Physical Optics

(a) red-light double-slit interference pattern; (b) constructive interference produces high red-light intensity on the screen and destructive interference leaves it dark; (c) plane wavefront geometry.
Physical Optics

EXPERIMENTAL ARRANGEMENT. Figure 9.9 shows Young’s double-slit setup. Monochromatic light from a source passes through a narrow vertical slit and falls on two other narrow slits A and B. A and B are very close together and parallel to C [the source’s final wording is partly clipped]. The slits A and B act as two coherent sources. A screen is placed a distance L beyond slits A and B.
Physical Optics

In Young’s experiment, interference is explained using Huygens’ principle. Slit C sends out circular wavefronts. Since slits A and B are equally distant from C, the same wavefront reaches both. Points at A and B emit wavelets in phase, so the emerging beams are coherent, with the same frequency and amplitude. This method of obtaining two coherent sources is called division of a wavefront.
Physical Optics

Because A and B are narrow, diffraction spreads the emerging light beyond the slits. Superposition of waves from A and B produces interference: solid lines give constructive interference and bright fringes; broken lines give destructive interference and dark fringes (Figure 9.8).
Physical Optics

To derive the separation of successive bright or dark fringes, consider Figure 9.9. d is the separation of slits A and B, L is the distance from the slits to the screen, and O is the screen’s central point. CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE. The path difference for waves from A and B reaching O is zero. They arrive in the same phase, so constructive interference and a bright fringe occur at O.
Physical Optics
A wave traveling from slit B to screen point P covers distance s farther than the wave from slit A. Figure 9.9: Young’s double-slit experimental setup.
Physical Optics

CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE. Point P is bright when path difference s is an integral multiple of wavelength: BP − AP = s = 0, λ, 2λ, … ; equivalently s = mλ, where m = 0, ±1, ±2, ±3, … . For Figure 9.9, s = BQ = d sin θ. Comparing gives d sin θ = mλ. At central point O, m = 0, producing the zero-order bright fringe. For m = ±1, first-order maxima occur above and below O.
Physical Optics
Figure 9.10(a) shows bright positions at integer multiples λL/d and dark positions at odd half multiples λL/(2d), 3λL/(2d), 5λL/(2d), … .
Physical Optics

DESTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE AT P. If path difference s between waves from A and B reaching P is an odd integral multiple of half a wavelength, they are 180° (π rad) out of phase. Destructive interference then occurs at P and a dark fringe is observed. Figure 9.10(b) shows constructive interference at P for equal paths; (c) constructive interference at P₁; and (d) destructive interference at P₂.
Physical Optics

For destructive interference, d sin θ = λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, …, equivalently d sin θ = (m + 1/2)λ, where m = 0, ±1, ±2, … . POSITION OF FRINGES ON THE SCREEN. To find the vertical distance y of the mth-order bright or dark fringe from the central point O, consider similar right-angled triangles ABQ and PEO: s/y = AB/PE = d/PE (i). In the experiment y ≪ L and PE ≈ EO = L, so s/y = d/L and y = Ls/d (9.3).
Physical Optics

FOR YOUR INFORMATION — BLUE SKY. Short wavelengths are scattered from the Sun’s direct beam more effectively at midday than longer wavelengths. These scattered waves produce the blue sky. We do not look directly at the Sun when seeing the sky; we see light scattered multiple times, concentrating shorter blue and violet wavelengths in the light reaching our eyes.
Physical Optics
Sunlight contains more blue than violet, and our eyes respond more strongly to blue than violet, so the colour we identify is blue. Figure: Sunbeam and scattered light.

(A) mth BRIGHT FRINGE. Substitute the constructive-interference path difference to obtain bright-fringe positions: (y)bright = 0, Lλ/d, 2Lλ/d, 3Lλ/d, … . Thus (yₘ)bright = mLλ/d (9.4).
Physical Optics
mth DARK FRINGE. Substituting the destructive-interference condition gives (y)dark = Lλ/(2d), 3Lλ/(2d), 5Lλ/(2d), … . Thus (yₘ)dark = (m + 1/2)Lλ/d (9.5).
Physical Optics

FRINGE SPACING. The distance between consecutive bright or dark fringes is fringe spacing. Between first- and second-order bright fringes: spacing = 2Lλ/d − Lλ/d = Lλ/d. Between first- and second-order dark fringes: spacing = 3Lλ/(2d) − Lλ/(2d) = Lλ/d. Therefore fringe spacing = Lλ/d (9.6).
Physical Optics
QUIZ. Young’s double-slit experiment divides one light beam into two sources. Would the same pattern occur with two independent light sources, such as headlights of a distant car?
Physical Optics

(a) ybright = mLλ/d = (1 × 5893 × 10⁻¹⁰)/0.001 = 5.893 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Physical Optics

EXAMPLE 9.2 · YOUNG’S INTERFERENCE. Light of wavelength 546 nm produces Young’s interference pattern. The second-order dark fringe lies at an angle of 18 minutes relative to the central maximum. Find slit separation. GIVEN: λ = 546 nm = 546 × 10⁻⁹ m; dark-fringe order m = 2; θ = 18 min = 18/60 = 0.30° (1° = 60 minutes). REQUIRED: d.
Physical Optics

For the mth dark fringe, d sin θ = (m + 1/2)λ, so d = (m + 1/2)λ/sin θ. Substituting: d = (2 + 1/2) × (546 × 10⁻⁹)/sin 0.30°. Since sin 0.30° = 5.236 × 10⁻³, d = 2.5 × (546 × 10⁻⁹)/(5.236 × 10⁻³) = 260.7 × 10⁻⁶ m = 260.7 μm. Answer: 260.7 μm.

9.7 INTERFERENCE IN THIN FILM. Colour bands on the surface of slightly oily water and soap bubbles on water are interference fringes caused by rays reflected from the upper and lower surfaces of a thin oil film on water. The principle uses division of amplitude by partial reflection and transmission at the boundary of two media. Consider a thin, wedge-shaped refracting film of refractive index as in Figure 9.11.
Physical Optics

A beam of monochromatic light of wavelength λ is incident on the film and splits into two parts. Ray a is reflected from the upper surface; ray b is reflected from the lower surface. Their separation is very small because the film is thin. Since both rays come from the same beam, they are coherent and superpose. Ray b travels farther than ray a.
Physical Optics

Their path difference depends on (i) the film’s thickness and nature and (ii) the angle of incidence. Figure 9.11 labels incident light, rays a and b, the eye, the medium, and the thin-film interference.
Physical Optics

(a) When a wave travels from a medium of lower refractive index to one of higher refractive index, it undergoes a 180° (π rad) phase change on reflection. (b) There is no phase change in the reflected wave when it travels from a medium of higher refractive index to one of lower refractive index.
Physical Optics

When white light falls at all possible angles on a thin film of irregular thickness, each spectral colour has its own interference pattern. At a place where the thickness and incidence angle satisfy destructive interference for one colour, the film shows the remaining white-light colours because different wavelengths reinforce at different places.
Physical Optics
Highly coloured fringes produce the rainbow effect in soap bubbles and oil films on water. The sidebar shows a soap bubble and states that its colours appear when sunlight falls on its surface.
Physical Optics

9.8 MICHELSON’S INTERFEROMETER. The Michelson interferometer is an optical instrument used to study interference of light waves and find their wavelength. Its principle is division of amplitude, usually by partial reflection and transmission at the boundary between two media. Its essential parts are two plane mirrors M₁ and M₂ and two glass plates A and B, as in Figure 9.12(a).
Physical Optics
Plate A is lightly silvered on its back, so half the incident light is reflected and half transmitted. Mirror M₁ is movable; mirror M₂ is fixed.
Physical Optics

Figure 9.12(a), ray diagram of the Michelson interferometer: monochromatic light from source S falls on plate A and splits. Beam 1 reflects from A toward movable mirror M₁, reflects there, transmits through A, and reaches the eye through the telescope. Beam 2 transmits through A toward fixed mirror M₂, reflects back to A, reflects there, and reaches the eye.
Physical Optics
Compensating plate B is placed in beam 2 to equalize the glass path lengths of beams 1 and 2. The figure labels L₁ and L₂, source, plates A/B, mirrors M₁/M₂, beams 1/2, and eye.
Physical Optics

CONDITIONS FOR INTERFERENCE. Constructive interference and brightness occur when the path difference d between the two parts of the light is zero or an integral multiple of wavelength λ: d = 0, λ, 2λ, 3λ, …; therefore d = mλ, where m = 0, 1, 2, 3, … (equation 9.7).
Physical Optics

DESTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE. Darkness occurs when the path difference is an odd integral multiple of half a wavelength: d = λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, …; equivalently d = (m + 1/2)λ, where m = 0, 1, 2, 3, … (equation 9.8). If mirrors M₁ and M₂ are equidistant from plate A, the beams travel optically similar paths. Plate B introduces in beam 2 the same retardation introduced in beam 1 by its two passages through A.
Physical Optics
Thus path difference is zero and a bright fringe occurs by constructive interference.
Physical Optics

ALTERNATE BRIGHT AND DARK FRINGES. If mirror M₁ is moved backward through λ/4, the path difference becomes λ/2 and a dark fringe appears. Moving it a further λ/4 makes the path difference λ and a bright band appears. Thus, as M₁ moves slowly by λ/4 each time, bright and dark fringes appear alternately. Figure 9.12(b) shows concentric fringes produced with a Michelson interferometer.
Physical Optics
WAVELENGTH OF LIGHT. If m fringes are observed while mirror M₁ is moved backward by λ/4 each time, total distance P = m(λ/4 + λ/4) = mλ/2. Therefore λ = 2P/m (equation 9.9). Knowing m and P gives λ.
Physical Optics

EXAMPLE 9.3 · SODIUM VAPOUR (as printed). A red laser of wavelength 630 nm is used in a Michelson interferometer. With M₁ fixed, mirror M₂ is moved and one fringe crosses a fixed cross-hair in the viewer. Find the distance M₂ moves. GIVEN: λ = 630 nm; m = 1. REQUIRED: distance P traveled by M₂. Using P = mλ/2 = (1 × 630)/2 nm = 315 nm. Printed answer: P = 315 nm.
Physical Optics

9.9 DIFFRACTION OF LIGHT. Waves do not always cast sharp shadows. In Young’s double-slit experiment, light bends from its straight path and spreads into the region beyond the slits that would otherwise be shadow. This occurs for all types of waves: sound spreads behind an obstacle or corner that hides its source because sound waves bend around it. Water waves on a smooth [sentence continues on the next page].
Physical Optics

Continuation: water waves in a pond or ripple tank do not cast a clear shadow of an object because the waves diffract. These familiar examples are rarely questioned. Light also exhibits diffraction, providing experimental evidence for its wave theory. Diffraction is the bending of waves around the edges of a narrow opening or obstacle into the region behind it.
Physical Optics
Light diffraction is observed when the opening or obstacle is so small that its size is comparable with the wavelength of the light used.
Physical Optics

FIGURE 9.13. Plane waves reach a narrow gap and spread out beyond it as curved wavefronts; the figure states that this spreading is diffraction and is most obvious when the gap is approximately the same size as the wavelength. FIGURE 9.14. Diffraction-fringe intensity against θ/radians:
Physical Optics
a broad central maximum at zero, smaller side maxima, and minima/fringes at labeled angular positions including ±λ/2, ±λ, ±3λ/2, and ±2λ.
Physical Optics

In Young’s double-slit experiment, light from slit C simultaneously illuminates slits A and B because light passing through narrow slit C bends around its corners and spreads through the region between C and A/B. (a) A monochromatic beam through a narrow slit produces diffraction; its central maximum is more intense and much broader than the other maxima.
Physical Optics
(b) A monochromatic source near a knife edge also shows diffraction; bending around the edge produces the pattern in Figure 9.14. The text then introduces two types of experiments.
Physical Optics

9.10 DIFFRACTION AT A SINGLE SLIT. Diffraction produced by a narrow slit when plane light waves are incident normally on it and the emerging waves are also plane is called Fraunhofer diffraction. To observe it, send light through a single slit and record transmitted light on photographic film, as in Figure 9.15(a). The central bright band is considerably wider than the slit.
Physical Optics
Other bright bands occur on each side of the central image, indicating an interference effect.
Physical Optics

FIGURE 9.15(a), single-slit diffraction: a light beam passes through one slit and forms a broad central bright image with narrower side bands on photographic film. Figure labels: light beam, single slit, photographic film, and “Single slit diffraction.”
Physical Optics

Consider plane wavefronts incident on narrow slit AB (Figure 9.15(b)). By Huygens’ principle each point on the slit wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. At screen point O on the perpendicular bisector, waves from A and B arrive in phase because they are equidistant; there is no path difference for A/B or X/Y, so constructive interference gives a bright fringe.
Physical Optics

For every point on wavefront AQ there is a symmetric point on QB; their wavelets reach O in phase and superpose to make a bright spot. At a point P below O, the path difference between wavelets from A and B is λ. The path differences for pairs A/Q, X/Y, and Q/B reaching P are each approximately λ/2. Figure labels A, M, X, θ, Q, Y, B, slit width d, O, P, screen, and diffraction fringes.
Physical Optics

For angle θ between QP and the slit axis, the first dark fringe follows from triangle AMQ: (d/2)sinθ = λ/2, so d sinθ = λ and d = λ/sinθ. For the mth order minima, sinθₘ = mλ/d, where m = 1, 2, 3, … (equation 9.10). Dark fringes also occur on the other side of axis QO; bright fringes lie between dark fringes. The central maximum is brightest and the other maxima have much lower intensity.
Physical Optics
For a narrow slit and small angle, θ = λ/d; reducing slit width increases θ and broadens the central maximum, while all bright fringes become less intense because less light passes through the slit.
Physical Optics

9.11 DIFFRACTION GRATING. A diffraction grating is used as a practical instrument for accurately measuring light wavelength; an instrument constructed for this purpose is called a grating spectrometer. A grating is basically a glass or plastic plate about 2–3 cm long and 2–3 mm thick, ruled with many parallel, equally spaced slits of the same width.
Physical Optics
It can be made by scratching parallel lines on transparent glass or plastic; the spaces between scratches transmit light and act as separate slits.
Physical Optics

A diffraction grating works by interference and diffraction of light and is used to measure wavelength. Light diffracted by its slits is allowed to interfere. Figure 9.16(a) shows a five-slit grating and its operation. A parallel monochromatic beam produces waves from every slit; in certain directions, waves from adjacent slits are in phase and reinforce.
Physical Optics

The diffracted parallel rays make angle θ with the normal and an achromatic lens focuses them at screen point P. If adjacent rays 1 and 2 differ in path by one wavelength λ, they reinforce at P. Waves from any two consecutive slits then have path difference λ and produce a bright fringe. Thus constructive interference requires Δr = λ (i).
Physical Optics

From Figure 9.16(b), Δr = d sinθ (ii), where d is the separation of adjacent slits. The figure labels five slits, rays 1/2, A/B/C, slit spacing d, angle θ, lens, screen points O/P, and the path geometry r.
Physical Optics

From Δr = λ and Δr = d sinθ, d sinθ = λ (iii). Here d is separation between adjacent slits, called the grating element: d = (unit length of grating)/(total number N of ruled lines); for a 1 cm unit, d = 1 cm/N. In other directions on either side of line OC, adjacent waves may differ in path by 2λ, 3λ, …, producing second-, third-order, etc. bright images.
Physical Optics
The general grating equation is d sinθ = mλ, where m = 0, 1, 2, 3, … is the order of the image.
Physical Optics

FOR YOUR INFORMATION. A grating spectrometer measures wavelength. Monochromatic light enters the grating normally through the collimator; diffracted light leaves at angle θ and a telescope views the image. Measuring angles of several orders on each side of the central maximum allows wavelength calculation. Figure labels:
Physical Optics
light source, slit, lens, collimator, grating, telescope, eye piece, first order on both sides, and zero order.
Physical Optics

EXAMPLE 9.4 · DIFFRACTED IMAGE. An optical grating has 5000 lines per centimetre; the deviation angle of the second-order image is 32°. Find wavelength λ. GIVEN: N = 5000 lines/cm, θ = 32°, m = 2. Grating element d = 1 cm/5000 = 0.00020 cm. From d sinθ = mλ, λ = d sinθ/m = (0.00020 cm × sin32°)/2 = (0.00020 × 0.53)/2 = 5.3 × 10⁻⁵ cm. Printed answer: 5.3 × 10⁻⁵ cm.
Physical Optics

9.12 THE DIFFRACTION OF X-RAYS BY CRYSTAL. Interference and diffraction are important for studying crystal structure. Atomic layers in crystals are less than 1 nm apart, so very short-wavelength radiation is needed. X-rays are electromagnetic waves with wavelength about 10⁻¹⁰ m. Their interference fringes cannot be produced by Young’s double-slit experiment or by the thin-film method.
Physical Optics
Figure 9.17 shows an X-ray source, lead barrier with opening W, collimator slit S, crystal C, and detector D; the diffracted ray and angles θ and 2θ are marked.
Physical Optics

The fringe spacing is Lλ/d; unless crystal-plane separation is of order 10⁻¹⁰ m, the fringes are too close to observe. X-ray diffraction can be obtained with sodium chloride (NaCl), common table salt. Crystal atoms are uniformly spaced in planes separated by distance d. FIGURE 9.18 shows X-ray diffraction patterns.
Physical Optics

In a typical Laue experiment (Figure 9.19), a narrow X-ray beam is collimated through a slit onto a crystal such as NaCl; the transmitted beam enters detector D. The Laue photograph has a central spot surrounded by many spots in a defined pattern, called Laue spots. Their arrangement differs with crystal structure.
Physical Optics
This experiment demonstrates that X-rays are electromagnetic waves and atoms are arranged in three-dimensional lattices.
Physical Optics

9.12.1 BRAGG’S LAW. Bragg’s law is used to find the wavelength of an X-ray beam using a crystal. To derive it, Figure 9.20 considers two parallel rays I and II incident on the first and second crystal layers. [Derivation continues on the following page.]
Physical Optics

In Figure 9.20 adjacent crystal planes are separated by d; θ is the glancing angle, complementary to the angle of incidence. Successive reflected rays reinforce when their path difference is an integral multiple of wavelength. Ray II travels farther than ray I by BC + CB′ = mλ (i). From the diagram BC = CB′ = d sinθ. Therefore 2d sinθ = mλ, where m = 1, 2, 3, … (equation 9.11), Bragg’s law.
Physical Optics

With known X-ray wavelength it determines crystal interplanar spacing; with known spacing it determines wavelength. X-ray diffraction has helped determine structures of biologically important molecules, including hemoglobin and DNA’s double helix.
Physical Optics

EXAMPLE 9.5 · X-RAYS OF WAVELENGTH. X-rays of wavelength 3 nm strike a crystal with lattice spacing 5 nm. Find the angle of the first Bragg diffraction. GIVEN: λ=3×10⁻⁹ m, d=5×10⁻⁹ m, m=1. From 2d sinθ=mλ, sinθ=(mλ)/(2d)=(1×3×10⁻⁹)/(2×5×10⁻⁹)=0.3; θ=17°. Printed answer: 17°. ASSIGNMENT 9.2: X-rays of wavelength 0.3 nm give a first-order maximum at glancing angle 9.0°. Find atomic spacing.
Physical Optics

9.13 POLARIZATION OF LIGHT. Interference and diffraction prove the wave nature of light, but alone do not show whether light waves are longitudinal or transverse. Polarization suggests that light waves are transverse. Polarization restricts the electric and magnetic vibrations of light to a single plane of vibration. It is a property of transverse waves only and does not occur for longitudinal waves such as sound.
Physical Optics

EXPERIMENT WITH TRANSVERSE WAVES. To show that only transverse waves exhibit polarization, let a transverse wave on a string pass through slot P in a board (Figure 9.21). A slot parallel to the transverse vibrations lets the wave pass undisturbed. If a second slot is at right angles to the first, no wave passes through it.
Physical Optics

Replacing the string by a spring carrying a longitudinal (compressional) wave lets the wave pass regardless of slot orientation; longitudinal waves therefore do not show polarization. The sidebar recommends polarized sunglasses over ordinary sunglasses.
Physical Optics

9.13.1 ORDINARY LIGHT. Why is ordinary light unpolarized? Light is emitted when an orbiting electron jumps from a higher to a lower energy state. A transition involving an electron in a vertical plane emits vertically polarized light; a horizontal orbit emits horizontally polarized light.
Physical Optics

Light from a candle flame, bulb filament, or Sun is unpolarized because it comes from many atoms whose electrons undergo transitions in different planes in all directions. [The source scan clips the right edge; the final phrase is incomplete.]
Physical Optics

Figure 9.22 and text: light is an electromagnetic wave with periodic electric-field vector E and magnetic-field vector B vibrations at right angles to each other. The diagram shows a light source emitting unpolarized light, a polarizing filter, and polarized light beyond it.
Physical Optics

9.13.2 PRODUCTION OF POLARIZED LIGHT. A plane-polarized beam can be obtained from unpolarized light by removing waves except those vibrating along one chosen direction. Methods: (i) selective absorption; (ii) reflection from a surface; (iii) refraction through crystals; (iv) scattering by tiny particles. Selective absorption is the common method:
Physical Optics
a dichroic Polaroid crystal made from tiny crystals of quinine iodosulphate transmits vibrations parallel to its crystallographic axis and absorbs the remaining vibrations.
Physical Optics

In the two-tourmaline experiment (Figure 9.23), ordinary unpolarized light from the source falls on the first tourmaline crystal; its molecular structure transmits only electric and magnetic vibrations parallel to its crystallographic axis and absorbs the rest.
Physical Optics

The first tourmaline transmits vibrations in one plane, producing plane-polarized light. A second tourmaline with its crystallographic axis parallel to the first transmits all the polarized light. Rotating the second crystal inclines the axes and decreases transmitted intensity; at 90° no light passes. Rotating it farther makes emergent light reappear.
Physical Optics

Thus the second crystal is an analyzer, and the arrangement produces a polarized beam. Figure 9.23(a) shows vertical axes and polarized light transmitted; (b) shows crossed horizontal/vertical positions and no light.
Physical Optics

9.13.3 POLARIZATION BY REFLECTION. Unpolarized light reflected from glass, water, etc. is generally partially plane-polarized. At a particular angle of incidence, the polarizing angle, polarization is complete. At this angle the reflected ray and refracted ray in the transmitted medium are at right angles. Vibrations in the reflected ray are parallel to the surface.
Physical Optics
The text begins applying Snell’s law; its resulting relation continues on the next page.
Physical Optics

Snell’s law at the polarizing angle iₚ is n₁ sin iₚ = n₂ sin r (9.12), where n₁ and n₂ are the absolute refractive indices of media 1 and 2. Figure 9.24 gives iₚ + 90° + r = 180°, hence r = 90° − iₚ. Substituting: n₁ sin iₚ = n₂ sin(90°−iₚ)=n₂ cos iₚ, so n₂/n₁ = sin iₚ/cos iₚ = tan iₚ (9.13), Brewster’s law. For glass of refractive index 1.55, the source gives iₚ = 57°.
Physical Optics

Figure 9.24 labels unpolarized incident ray, totally plane-polarized reflected ray, partially plane-polarized refracted ray, media 1/2, incidence/reflection angles iₚ, refraction angle r, and their 90° relation.
Physical Optics

9.13.4 APPLICATIONS OF POLARIZED LIGHT — REDUCING GLARE. Glare reflected from smooth surfaces such as roads and lakes can be reduced with polarizing materials because reflected light is partially or completely polarized. Properly oriented Polaroid discs in sunglasses block the polarized glare. In photography, Polaroid discs in front of the camera lens reveal detail otherwise hidden by glare.
Physical Optics
The sidebar says reflected light from glass is partially polarized and that horizontally polarized reflected glare is absorbed by sunglasses, allowing vertically polarized light through.
Physical Optics

OPTICAL ACTIVITY. When light passes through certain crystals (quartz) or liquids (sugar solution), the vibration direction of transmitted polarized light is rotated; this is optical activity. For a solution, rotation angle depends on concentration.
Physical Optics
A polarimeter measures the rotation and is used to determine solution concentration; sugar mills use polarimeters to measure the sugar concentration of cane-derived solution.
Physical Optics

(iii) CURTAINLESS WINDOW. Fix two polarizing sheets in a window, one inside and one outside; rotate the inner sheet to adjust admitted light. (iv) CONTROL OF HEADLIGHT GLARE. Safe night driving is possible with polarizing headlights on cars and a polarized-light viewer; Polaroid glasses eliminate glare that is partly polarized by reflection from water and roads. (v) STRESS ANALYSIS.
Physical Optics

Stressed glass, polythene and other plastics (bent, twisted, or unevenly heated) become doubly refracting. Viewed in white light between crossed Polaroids, coloured fringes appear around strained regions. This photoelasticity is used to analyze stress in plastic models of structures.
Physical Optics

KEY POINTS — Nature of light: modern view is dual; light behaves as a wave in reflection and refraction and as particles in photoelectric and Compton effects. Wavefront: locus of medium points in the same phase. Ray: arrow showing wavefront direction; rays are perpendicular to wavefronts. Phase-coherent sources maintain a constant phase relationship between their emitted waves. Interference:
Physical Optics

effect of superposing two coherent waves. Diffraction: bending of light waves around an obstacle and spreading into its geometrical shadow. Polarization: restricting the electric and magnetic vibrations of light to one plane.

THERMODYNAMICS. “Thermo” relates to heat and “dynamics” to motion of particles. Thermodynamics is the branch of physics dealing with laws for transformation of heat into other forms of energy—mechanical, chemical, electrical—and vice versa. It is principally based on the first and second laws. It explains operation of heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps.

System, surroundings, boundary and state variables have specific meanings in thermodynamics. Sidebar: William Rankine, originally trained as a physicist and a civil and mechanical engineering professor at the University of Glasgow, wrote the first thermodynamics textbook in 1859.

10.2 WORK. Work W is defined as F⃗·Δs⃗. In thermodynamics, a system does work when it expands as a whole: through its boundary it exerts force on the surroundings and displaces them. The sum of F⃗·Δs⃗ over the entire boundary is work done by the system on its surroundings. During contraction, surroundings do work on the system. By convention, work done by the system is positive and work done on it is negative.

10.3 INTERNAL ENERGY. Atoms and molecules of matter are in constant motion. Atoms in solids vibrate about equilibrium positions; molecules in liquids move among one another and collide, exchanging energy; gas molecules travel at high speed and undergo frequent elastic collisions. The sum of kinetic and potential energies associated with random atomic motion is the substance’s internal energy.
Thermodynamics

Kinetic energy can be translational, rotational, or vibrational. Heating a substance increases random motion and associated energy, converting heat energy into internal energy. Work can also increase atomic random motion and be converted into internal energy. Once heat, work, or both enter a substance, they are no longer distinguishable there. QUIZ:

10.4 HEAT, WORK AND INTERNAL ENERGY. Heat, work and internal energy are distinct concepts, each related to body temperature. Heating water on a flame or placing an object in thermal contact with a hotter object raises its temperature. Earth is heated by the Sun without direct thermal contact.
Thermodynamics

In these processes something flows from the hotter body to the colder body until their temperatures become equal; this is called heat. Heat is energy transferred between a substance and surroundings, or between parts of a substance, solely because of a temperature difference. Heat is energy in transit and flows until bodies in thermal contact reach equal temperatures. Its SI unit is joule (J).
Thermodynamics
A common unit is the calorie (cal), defined as energy needed to raise 1.00 g of water by 1.00°C, specifically from 14.5°C to 15.5°C.
Thermodynamics

A kilocalorie (kcal) is the energy needed to raise 1.00 kg of water by 1.00°C. Besides supplying heat, work on a body can raise its temperature: rubbing hands, hammering a nail into wood, churning curd, and pumping a tyre with a hand pump. In each, work warms a body without heat supply. Heat and work can both raise temperature but are mutually distinct energy-transfer forms.
Thermodynamics

Work is exchanged through overall displacement and does not require a temperature difference; heat transfer requires a temperature difference. QUIZ: A small drill boring hard board becomes hot—why? What changes with soft board? Why do sparks occur when stones collide?

10.4.1 EQUIVALENCE OF HEAT AND WORK. Count Rumford, James Joule and others established equivalence. In 1798, artillery engineer Count Rumford observed heat released while boring gun metal; friction could produce heat exhaustively by mechanical work. The heat was not related to the mass of metal removed, but to work done against friction, leading Rumford to conclude heat is a form of energy.
Thermodynamics
In 1845 Joule precisely measured heat produced by a certain amount of mechanical work and observed a definite relationship between work and heat. [The sentence continues on the following page.]
Thermodynamics

Joule showed that the same amount of work always produces the same amount of heat, regardless of the transformation process. Work W is proportional to heat Q: W∝Q; W=JQ. J is the mechanical equivalent of heat (Joule’s constant), defined as work in joules divided by heat produced in calories, or as mechanical energy required to produce one unit of heat. Its accepted value is J=4.18 joules/calorie.
Thermodynamics
If work and heat are both measured in joules (SI), the mechanical equivalent is 1.

10.6 REVERSIBLE AND IRREVERSIBLE PROCESSES. In thermodynamics, a process is a change in a system’s state caused by a change in state variables. A process occurs when a system interacts and exchanges energy with surroundings.
Thermodynamics

REVERSIBLE PROCESS. A process is reversible if retraced exactly in reverse without changing surroundings. The system passes through the same states; thermal and mechanical effects at each stage are exactly reversed. Heat absorbed in the forward process is released in reverse; work done by the system forward is done on it in reverse.
Thermodynamics

No real process is exactly reversible, but sufficiently slow processes can be treated as such. Slow liquefaction/evaporation and slow gas compression are examples; slow pressure reduction reverses compression into expansion. IRREVERSIBLE PROCESS: cannot be retraced backward by reversing controlling factors.
Thermodynamics

Sudden changes and processes involving friction or energy dissipation by conduction, convection or radiation are irreversible; explosion is highly irreversible. CYCLIC PROCESS: a sequence returning the system to its initial state; a system undergoing cycles is often a heat engine.
Thermodynamics

10.7 FIRST LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS. Energy cannot be created or destroyed in a thermodynamic system; this law is a heat-energy form of conservation of energy. Every thermodynamic system has state variable U, internal energy. In a process, added heat ΔQ appears as increased stored internal energy ΔU plus work ΔW done by the system on surroundings: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW.
Thermodynamics

Equation 10.1: ΔQ=ΔU+ΔW. ΔQ is positive when heat enters the system and negative when it leaves. ΔU is positive when temperature rises and negative when it falls. The first law combines (1) internal energy U as a state variable, (2) conservation of energy, and (3) heat as energy in transit.
Thermodynamics

Internal energy is the sum of kinetic (translational, rotational, vibrational) and potential energies associated with random atomic motion. ISOTHERMAL EXPANSION. Slowly reduce pressure on the piston so gas expands and tends to cool; heat flows from the reservoir to keep system temperature equal to reservoir temperature T. The path from (P₁,V₁,T) to (P₂,V₂,T) is a continuous curve, an “isotherm” (Figure 10.7). During expansion the gas does work ΔW; since temperature is constant, ΔU=0. First law: ΔQ=ΔU+ΔW=ΔW.

Thus equal heat must enter when gas expands and does external work; when it contracts, work is done on it and equal heat leaves. ADIABATIC PROCESS: no heat enters or leaves the system, so ΔQ=0. For a practical adiabatic process, use a completely insulated cylinder with movable piston; no heat enters or leaves, so ΔQ=0. Thus an internal-energy increase equals work done on the system; if the system does work during adiabatic expansion, it is at the cost of internal energy. 10.9 HEAT ENGINE. A heat engine converts heat energy into mechanical work; steam, petrol and diesel engines are examples. A heat engine has these parts. Heat source or reservoir: a very large high-temperature body at T₁ whose temperature stays practically unchanged during heat transfer; also called the high-temperature reservoir (HTR). Heat sink or cold reservoir:
Thermodynamics

a very large low-temperature body at T₂ whose temperature likewise remains practically unchanged; also called the low-temperature reservoir (LTR). Working substance: normally a gas. The substance undergoes a cyclic process, absorbs heat Q₁ from the source at T₁, does maximum work W on the surroundings and rejects heat Q₂ to the sink at T₂ (Figure 10.12).
Thermodynamics

At the end of a complete cycle the system returns to its original internal energy, so ΔU=0. The first law gives ΔQ=ΔU+ΔW=ΔW. Thus for one cycle ΔW=Q₁−Q₂ (10.11). Thermal efficiency definition continues at the bottom edge [source line clipped]. Figure 10.12 labels: hot reservoir at T₁, Q₁, engine, W, Q₂, cold reservoir at T₂; schematic representation of a heat engine.
Thermodynamics

Heat-engine thermal efficiency is work done by the engine in each cycle divided by heat Q₁ absorbed in each cycle: η=ΔW/Q₁ (10.12). Using ΔW=Q₁−Q₂ gives η=(Q₁−Q₂)/Q₁=1−Q₂/Q₁ (10.13). If Q₂=0, all absorbed heat would be converted to work and η=1=100%. Experiments show that a 100% efficient heat engine is impossible: a steam, gasoline or diesel engine must reject some heat Q₂ to the heat sink (LTR).
Thermodynamics

One statement of the second law: no heat engine can have as its sole result the extraction of heat from a reservoir and production of an equal amount of work. A high-temperature source and low-temperature sink are essential for converting heat into mechanical work. During a complete cycle heat cannot all become useful work: an engine converts part into work and rejects the remainder to the sink. Thus work output is less than absorbed heat and efficiency is always below 100%. 10.10.2 RUDOLF CLAUSIUS STATEMENT:

It is impossible to cause heat to flow from a cold body to a hot body without expenditure of work. The first law describes heat and work as equivalent forms of energy; the second law concerns conversion of heat into work. For a cyclic process, the first law forbids getting more work from an engine than the heat supplied; the second law says work performed is less than heat absorbed. 10.11 CARNOT HEAT ENGINE.
